maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: With your leave, Mr. Speaker, in view of the adoption of daylight saving by several of our municipalities, and in view of the change in the time table of the railway systems of this country, might I ask the Acting Prime Minister what the Government intends to do in the matter having regard to the vote of this House last week?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext:
The Inside and Outside Civil Service has always conformed to local municipal regulations with regard to time. Therefore the Civil Service will, so far as practicable, conform to local time as established by municipal regulation.
With regard to the sessions of Parliament, which now begin every afternoon at three o'clock, except upon Wednesdays, when the session begins at two o'clock standard time, it has not yet been intimated to thp Government what official action will be "taken by the city of Ottawa;-that we shall know by to-morrow.
We also desire to await the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners on the question of railway time tables, which will be before it for consideration to-morrow! The House will therefore meet to-morrow by standard time, as it has met to-day. After we have received official information as to the action taken by the City of Ottawa 
and the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners, I shall announce to the House the course which will be suggested by the Government with respect to the hour of the meeting of Parliament, having regard to the convenience of members.

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: I should like to ask a question concerning another aspect of this matter. Railway corporations undoubtedly have the right to change their time tables, but has the Government considered what authority these corporations have for. changing the time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: That question is .at present before the Board tof Railway Commissioners for determination.

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: They may change their time tables, but not the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: I understand that it is the question of change of time tables that is before the Board of Railway Commissioners.

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: Is it the question of time tables, or the question of a change of time on the part of the railway companies? Any railway system may change its time table, but they may not change the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext:
The railways have changed the time and that question will come before the Board of Railway Commissioners to-morrow for determination as they may deem proper.

speechtext:

maintopic: MILITARY SERVICE ACT DEFAULTERS.
speechtext: Is the Acting Minister of Justice aware of the feeling of unrest which prevails throughout the country because of the imprisonment of young men who are unable to pay the $500 fine imposed by the last Order in Council with reference to defaulters under the Military Service Act? Is it the intention of the Government to take less drastic steps in this matter or to grant a general amnesty to all concerned ?

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: MILITARY SERVICE ACT DEFAULTERS.
speechtext: The Government is not aware, so far as I know, of any very general unrest in this connection. The question of amendment of the regulations and of the law is, of course, one thing, while the question of amnesty or clemency is another. Certain well-defined rules have been adapted on the latter subject, which, I think, do not err on the side of being too drastic. The matter of amendment to the law is not under immediate consideration.

speechtext:
On the Orders of the Day:
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia): As a matter of public interest I wish to advise the House as to the progress of demobilization up to date.
So far during the month of March we have moved from overseas and demobilized 42,232 soldiers and 4,850 dependents. In addition to that, 8,078 soldiers are now on the ocean.
Since the date of the armistice, up to and including to-day, including five ships now on the ocean, we have brought back 109,248 soldiers. Including those in Canada we have demobilized since November 11, the date of the armistice, 164,621 men.

speechtext:
MOTION BY MR. MeCURDY THAT WOUNDED SOLDIERS BE GIVEN PREFERENCE.
Mr. F. B. MeCURDY (Colchester) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Civil Service Act should be amended so that, while having full regard to efficiency, a preference in appointments to the public service shall be afforded to imemlbers of the Canadian Expeditionary Force who have become casualties in a theatre of war.
He said: All hon. members know that from 1914 to 1917, while appeals were being pressed on the manhood of Canada to voluntarily enlist in the military forces, undertakings both direct and implied were given from every recruiting platform to those who were being urged to join. Intending recruits were assured that, come good, come ill, Canada would see that after the war every reasonable consideration would at all times be afforded to those who responded to the call. I confidently state that these commitments were made with the practically unanimous consent of all Canada. And furthermore, were a similar world condition to confront Canada to-morrow, and should it become necessary to raise a large army by voluntary enlistment, I have no doubt that similar undertakings would again unhesitatingly be given.
The Government has not been at all idle in preparing to honour the country's obligations. It has created a good deal of machinery designed to facilitate the return of the soldier to civil life. It has provided medical and instructional services, established an elaborate pensioning system, and is now engaged in the establishment of a Soldiers' Land Settlement organization. But much remains to be done, and it must be particularly remembered that the best results can be assured only when all agencies dealing with the problem are fully or-ordinated and harmonized. For the purpose at which this resolution is aimed, the practice of the Civil Service Commission must undoubtedly be in concord with the policy of the Government.
Quite recently I was requested to make inquiry of the Civil Service Commission regarding the appointment of an officer in the public service in Nova Scotia. In response to notices sent out by the Commission two applications had been lodged. Both were from discharged soldiers, one having got as far as England and from
there returned to Canada for discharge, while the other, who had been wounded in France, had incurred a permanent partial disability of his left hand. Somewhat to my surprise I learned that, in practice, both these classes of returned soldiers were regarded by the Commissioners as possessing equal claims to appointment so far as their service records were concerned. That, the Commissioners advised, was the interpretation placed on the Civil Service Act. While we all appreciate the admirable spirit that impelled those who did not get further than England-as it did others- to enlist, it is undoubtedly in the public mind that those active service men who have sacrificed and suffered most best deserve preferment at the Government's hands. I am advised that in view of the decision of the Civil Service Commissioners, any alteration or rectification in cases such as I have referred to can be effected only by amendment to the Civil Service Act.
I will not give any opinion as to whether or not the Civil Service Commission are correctly interpreting the Civil Service Act, or whether or not they are following the policy of the Government in this matter. If they are facilitating a Government policy, then I am bound to say that in my opinion the Government has not correctly interpreted the opinion of hon. members of this House. Indeed, if the Civil Service Act really bore the interpretation that the Commission has placed upon it I feel that the Government would have been supported by this House in altering by Order in Council under the W'ar Measures Act this detail in order that the most deserving class should be fully protected. However, what is past is gone, and I am advised that it will largely meet the present situation if hon. members will support the resolution proposed. To them I confidently appeal.
In urging the particular claims of those who have become casualties, I do not for a moment wish to prejudice the rights,- already acknowledged by statute,-of any other one who has been on active service. I am satisfied that the purpose can be accomplished without creating any injustice anywhere.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would ask: Is it not eminently .fitting that, efficiency granted, the public service of Canada should, to as great an extent as possible be carried on by those who have already served their country in a vastly more difficult and sterner field of activity? And, asa matter of course, those who in the discharge of their military duties had incurred physical disabilities would, I take it, be
as gladly supported for preference by the public generally, as they are by their equally gallant but more fortunate unwounded comrades.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Would there be any objection to extending the resolution to include Canadians who have served in the British Expeditionary Force and in the Air Service?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
As I said some time ago, the main problem underlying the demobolization of our returned soldiers is that of employment. This is a duty which the people of Canada must seriously consider, if we are to avoid any difficulties with our returned men. The Government must also regard it as a duty which they owe these men, because they were instrumental in sending them overseas. When the State undertakes the disposition of certain classes of its citizens in various fields of activity, and, as in this case, send men to war, they must assume responsibility for the care of those who return with disabilities that handicap or prejudice them in the occupations which they formerly followed.
I think, further, that it is perfectly reasonable to say that returned soldiers should go into the Civil Service. Ordinarily, we do not recommend our friends to go into the Civil Service, but men who have been overseas for the last three or four years, who have suffered somewhat in their mental capacity because of their experiences and the shocks which they have received, or who have suffered physical disabilities, require that sense of security and steadiness which can be obtained in the Civil Service, perhaps, to a greater extent than any other line of activity in Canada. The Government, as the hon. member who has just spoken has stated, has given promises in that regard and I feel that the Government will take exactly the same view of this matter that they took when they made those promises.
I have no fault to find with the administration of the Civil Service Commission, but I do say that the Civil Service Act is not as well suited as it might be to the purpose of giving to returned men employment in the Civil Service. That Act was passed last year. I think I am correct in saying that every hon. member of this House is anxious that all returned soldiers who desire to enter the Civil Service, having regard to the efficiency of the service, should be given that opportunity. I think

the House will be willing to consider how the Act passed last year has fulfilled the desire of the House and the country in regard to the employment in the Civil Service of returned soldiers. Previous to the passing of this Act, and under the old patronage system, every member gave the positions coming under his control to returned men. Under the old system the member was amenable to the pressure of public opinion and he was directly responsible to the returned soldiers and to the people in his own community. Did that system still obtain, returned soldiers would to-day have practically all the positions in the Civil Service which become vacant. But, under the Civil Service Act, that element of responsibility on the member of Parliament has been eliminated.
We might look for a moment to see what the results have been under the Civil Service Act since that Act has been in force. We find by the figures which have been issued by the Civil Service Commission itself, that the following appointments have been made since the Act came into force:-
Permanent	 1,672
Temporary	! [	1C570
Total	 16,242
Of that 16,242 appointments made in one year 1,834 were returned soldiers. I must say in fairness to the commissioners that a large number of these appointments were stenographers which is a class of employment in which the soldier does not as a rule compete. However, I think that these figures in themselves are a fair indication of the truth of what I say. I do not believe that the returned soldiers are getting a sufficient number of positions in the Government service under the Civil Service Act which Parliament passed last year. The first point in the Act which I think might well be amended is this. It is provided by paragraph (a) of section 39 of the Civil Service Act that soldiers who have obtained sufficient marks in examination to pass shall be placed on the list at the head of all other candidates.
While it is true that many civilians are being appointed to positions in the Civil Service, the Commission have been doing what they could to provide soldiers with the necessary qualifications with positions.. But, especially in the West advertisements come out only a day or so ahead of the time that a man must send in his return in order that it may be received within the prescribed limit of time. We have coming back to Canada some 500,000 men and I do not think I will be going too far when I ask

this House to put it up to the Civil Service Commission to confine the appointment of male employees to returned soldiers. If that were put up to them they would know exactly where they stood, and they could send out the notices as to vacancies earlier. They might use the machinery of the Soldiers Civil Re-Establishment department, act through their labour representative in each district and get in touch with the returned soldier who might be available so that when a position is open a soldier will be ready for it. We might amend this Act for one year; or, we might amend it from year to year so that the condition would not extend for a longer time than was necessary, but for one year at least we might provide that none but returned soldiers should be allowed to compete in an examination where male employees are required. That is the first proposition I would make. Perhaps some honourable members may think that in proposing that I am going too far, but even if they take that viewpoint I would say to them that such a position would be much easier to maintain than the present position, which is certainly not going far enough.
Under section 15 of the Civil Service Act it is provided that the Civil Service Commission may appoint to positions requiring technical or professional knowledge without examination. That refers to positions requiring the knowledge of some profession or some other kind of technical knowledge. The Commission themselves, I must say, have gone as far as they could under that provision. They are not appointing without competitive examination all the people requiring technical or professional knowledge but they are as far as possible holding competitive examinations under that section. But there are under that clause, positions which are being filled without any examination and when no examination is held no preference is given returned soldiers. The Stead case, which was discussed in the House a few days ago, came under section 15 of the Act. While a competitive examination is required for all the lower positions in the service, and while it is in this class that preference is given to soldiers, in dealing with technical or professional positions no preference whatever is given to soldiers and we have the Stead case as an illustration of this. In addition to that, in the city of Calgary, we had some time ago, a civilian young man appointed to the position of assistant receiver general. There is no question in the world that a soldier could have been obtained properly qualified and trained to
fill that position. Nothing to my mind creates such a feeling of distrust or sense of unfairness among soldiers as to see a young civilian appointed to a position which a soldier could have filled. Usually that feeling is not manifested on the part of the particular soldier who wanted the position but on the part of other soldiers who have returned and who feel that it is the duty of the Government to provide for those who are not quite so well able to fight their own battles as those who have not suffered the shock of war. If there is any one thing that causes a feeling of distrust on the part of the soldiers, it is the appointment-in violation of the promises which this Government and this Parliament have made-of a civilian to a position which a soldier could have filled.
There is no preference whatever given to the dependents of soldiers. We should not throw the preference open to all relatives of soldiers but there is one class of soldiers' dependents who are well defined, a class who are in effect wards of the State, and that is the class who are obtaining pensions. By paying them pensions we admit that their male relatives, on whom they ar.e dependent for support, have either been killed or have received such injuries in the war that these dependents have been deprived of their means of support.
I think that this Act should contain a clause that those soldiers' dependents who are receiving a pension should be put in the same class as soldiers in competitive examinations and have the same preference as they have. In the case of soldiers there really is no age limit because any one who has been admitted into the army lias to undergo a medical examination and is pronounced quite fit and able to carry on, but as to dependents there would have to be an age limit.
Another point that has created a great deal of difficulty is that of promotion. Section 45 of the Act provides that :
Vacancies shall be filled, as far as consistent with the best interests of the Civil Service, by promotion.
Now we must all admit that promotions within the Civil Service should be a very tower of strength to it-that is to say, the hope of promotion should inspire the civil servant with ambition, and with the desire to do better work. But the soldiers' viewpoint is this: Under the present Civil Service Act practically every higher position in the Civil Service is being filled by promotion, and when we explain that to the soldiers they say. "When we went away, these positions used to be filled on the

recommendation of the local member; you tell us that you are going to give all vacant positions to soldiers; and yet you ask us to consider a scheme whereby you argue us out of these appointments, and the only positions we can get to-day in the Civil Service are the very lowest ones, and not all of those." In Calgary a famous case came up famous as far as I was concerned because even yet, although it happened a year and a quarter ago, protests against that appointment have not ceased. That was an appointment made to the Banff Park superintendency, which was made clearly in accordance with the Civil Service Act. Previously that position had been filled on the recommendation'of the member for the constituency, as I think practically all other appointments in the Outside Service were made. To-day, however, those appointments are made by promotion, and my view is that it would only be fair to the soldiers to say that hereafter these appointments should be given to them, and not only that but they should be eligible for those positions which are now regarded as promotions under the Act. Of course that could only go on for a year or two until the soldiers are absorbed into civil life, and my idea in urging this is that in the meantime the soldiers shall not suffer.
At the present time there are two classes of casualties in the country going to make up the total of two hundred thousand in our Army. The first class consists of those men who were wounded but that recovered to such an extent that their ability to carry on their ordinary work is by no means impaired. The second class consists of those whose wounds have been such as to unfit them in varying degrees to carry on their previous occupation. I feel, as the hon. member who proceeded me felt, that even over other spldiers the preference should be given to these casualties. That class can be very easily defined: they are the class to whom we pay pensions and an exact limit can be placed upon them. Not only should we give them a preference over other soldiers, but I think we should go even further. We should, if necessary, provide positions for these disabled men, not by making new positions, but by granting power to the Civil Service Commission to dismiss, if necessary, young men who had been appointed to the Civil iServiee since 1914, when war broke out. Let me make my position clear: I think that the Civil Service Commission should have the right to use their best discretion and select for dismissal, as likely to do the least harm, the young 
unmarried man, who was appointed while the war was in progress, and replace him by a soldier who has been so disabled that he is unable to carry on his previous avocation. That is, perhaps, a drastic proposition to make, but I believe it to be the duty of this Government towards these men who^ have been disabled in the country's service. I believe the Government can do that without any great amount of unfairness to any individual who was so appointed, and without violating any principle.

speechtext: Will the hon. member kindly define what he means by a "casualty"?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Technically it means any one who has appeared in the Army Orders as a casualty.
Sir 6AM HUGHES: You do not include shell-shocked men in that category.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
No. Such a man is not an offcial casualty. One would have to be a mind reader to determine all such cases.
Sir SAM HUGHES': That is the point I want to see explained.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
There may be cases that are not casualties that are suffering from these disabilities, and if any way could be devised to include them in the classes of men meriting better treatment, I should be only too pleased.
I have enumerated the different points I had in my mind with respect to this matter. I want to make it perfectly clear that I am not indulging in any criticism of the Government, or of the iCivil Service; I am simply pointing out to the House the defects which I think exist in the Act passed last year, defects which should be remedied since we all have the intention of doing full justice to the returned soldier.
I do not think anything which I have suggested will weaken in any way the efficiency of the service. It is rather a question of seeing that those who are more entitled than others to positions in.
4 p.m. the Civil Service are given that preference to which they deserve. I do not think there is anything to-day which is causing more distrust amongst returned soldiers than the appointment of young civilians to positions in the Civil Service.
Sir	SAM	HUGHES:	I	heartily
endorse the views expressed by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Redman) and the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy).
I would go a little further and broaden the

word casualty so as to include those who saw active service in the trenches that is men who fought in the trenches-because the fact that a man may have got a slight wound in the arm does not give him any better claim to a position over the soldier who fought alongside him for three years and happened to miss being hit. But that is merely a detail, which is covered by the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary.
I want to point out-while II am sorry to see the returned soldiers all looking for Civil Service positions, I would rather see them take their place in the broad fields of life and become more useful citizens to the country than civil servants can possibly become-that the remarks of the gentleman (Mr. Redman) are worthy of most serious consideration. I have been making inquiries throughout the country, as to whether the soldiers who have returned from the trenches have been reinstated in their old positions by the employers, or have taken other work, and with one or two exceptions, where men had been more or less disturbed by shell-shock, I have received most gratifying reports. I was speaking to the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) the other night and he mentioned that every man who had returned to his service, and he has many of them, is an infinitely better man than he was before he went overseas. As an old educator 1 have always been opposed to technical examinations for promotion, and I think that every educator in the country, who has studied the matter, will agree that technical examinations constitute no test of efficiency whatever, or very little. I would like to have the Government consider the matter from that viewpoint, that is, instead of having an applicant examined for a position by gentlemen who know nothing about the qualities of a soldier and mighty little about the duties of the office to which the applicant is aspiring, that these examinations should be limited practically to returned soldiers, and that the commission should give the benefit on every occasion to the returned soldier who is applying. Because, mark my words, the man coming back from the front is a much stronger and better man, nine times out of ten, except by reason of his physical incapacity, than if he had never gone to the war. The best men are those who had gone through the furnace of war
I would also like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that it would be well to have regard to the honourable casualty. There are casualties that are not
very creditable but, thank fortune, they aj*(j very verv few. A friend was telling me about a man who had made a great to-do about getting a position. My friend asked him for his medical sheet and his service record-his crime report; he never got them, and the man ceased applying. He had not been to the front at all. I think it would be well to make sure that we are getting the very best of these splendid fellows appointed to these positions. I thought all these positions were being filled by returned soldiers, and I was very much surprised to hear that that is not being done. I think the returned soldier is entitled to everything that can be given to him. I suggest that the motion should be enlarged so as to take in the men who have served at the front.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT JAMES MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I wish to support the motion of the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) and the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Redman). My recollection of the passing of this Civil Service Bill was that if say ten men passed the examination for a Civil Service appointment, and one of those men was a returned soldier, that he, would be given the preference, no matter where he stood on the examination list. If I understood wrongly, then I think such a rule should be put in force.
The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) made a point during the debate to the effect that the Canadians who had enlisted in the Imperial forces should be considered in filling these positions. I think any resolution to be passed by this House should embrace those men. I believe in filling all these positions with returned men. For instance, supposing in my constituency there is a vacancy in the Civil Service, but there is not in the neighbouring constituency an eligible man, I think some effort should be made to get a returned soldier from some other part of Canada for that position.
There is one little point more or less in connection with this that I would like to mention here. It is in regard to returned soldiers already working in some branch of the Civil Service. In my city at the present time a number of men on the grain inspection staff are laid off after the rush of the season is over. East year and the year before among the men laid off were a number of returned soldiers. The Great War Veterans' Association opposed this very vigorously, and perhaps they de-

mantled more than the department could see its way to give, because I think the department wanted to be quite fair to these men. On each occasion I brought the case to the notice of the department in charge, and I explained that I thought they should keep on an efficient staff, and that in addition they should keep on, even at a loss, any returned soldiers who were working on that staff. In the past year out of 80 men between Fort William, Port Arthur and Winnipeg, it only meant keeping on some ten or fifteen returned soldiers. That may seem unreasonable, but we as members of this Parliament have been asking the private corporations of this country to do that very thing, and, to be consistent, the least we can do is to ask our Government to do the same. It is boo late to remedy this matter this year. No doubt the department acted in good faith on the advice of its officials, but I believe that advice was wrongly given. I told the men who gave this advice in Fort William that I thought they gave it wrongly. They did not mean to be unfair, but they were unfair to the returned soldiers. I hope next year those returned soldiers will be retained in their positions as far as possible. I do not like to go so far as to suggest that other men should be laid off to give positions to returned soldiers, but I do not think returned soldiers should be laid off when we are asking private corporations to retain them.
One word in regard to shell shock, although there has been no extended discussion on that subject. Many men who have suffered from shell shock at the front are just as much casualties as the men who have been wounded. I have seen men come into my dugout in the front line who had seen some man wounded beside them; they were not wounded, but their nervous system was so completely shot to pieces, that they were in a much worse condition perhaps than the wounded man. Many of these cases are marked "shell shock wound" and are given a stripe to denote it, and a very large percentage deserve that stripe. I support very strongly the hon. members for Colchester and Calgary and hope that this resolution will carry.
/Hon. MAKTIN BURRELL (Secretary of State): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) has laid a resolution before the House which in fact advances the principle of a preference within a preference. It demands the sympathy of the House with respect to the matters it deals with, and that sympathy will not be any the less by reason of the fact that the [Mr. Man ion. 1
resolution has been spoken to by two members of this House, both of whom have done gallant service at the front, and not . on]y have they distinguished themselves there, but they have created a most favourable impression in this House.
I call the attention of the House to the fact that a resolution bearing on this matter was brought down by the hon. member for North Grey in 1916, though it did not go as far as the resolution now under discussion. That resolution read:
That, in the opinion of this House, in all future appointments to the Civil Service of Canada, preference should be given to those properly qualified candidates who have served with the Canadian Expeditionary Force in the present war.
Although that resolution only spoke of a preference for Canadian soldiers generally, the hon. member who brought the resolution before the House at that time made this statement:
As all those who return will not be able to secure appointments in the Civil Service, we shall have to create a preferential class among them, and in doing so, no doubt we shall take into consideration the fact that those who have been wounded, but who after a certain time will be able to perform the duties appertaining to civil servants, should be given preferential ti eatment among those who have served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
The Prime Minister also spoke in that debate and referred to the Order in Council which was passed on November 27, 1917: It is as follows:
-	 wu. uic x uvj1 uuuuun, on tne
recommendation of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister, advise that in making appointments to the Government Civil Service, preference be given to the returned members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, especially those who through disability occasioned by active military service are unable to fill their previous occupations; such appointments to be subject to the provisions of the Civil Service Act and to be made with due regard to the capacity of any applicant to discharge the duties of the position to which it is proposed to appoint him.
Subsequently, as hon. members know, a provision was put in the Civil Service Act which, while not going as far, perhaps, as the resolution proposed by my hon. friend, did give general preference to returned soldiers. I sympathize with the view of my hon. friend, supported by the member for Calgary (Mr. Redman) that the policy of the Civil Service Commission should be in accord with the principles enunciated in that provision and laid down by the members who have just spoken. Of course, the mover of the resolution and the member for Calgary must recognize as we all do, the difficulties which surround this ques-

tion. I am sure that the Civil Service Commission are doing the best they can. Of course, there will be mistakes. Some time ago objection was raised because returned soldiers who were applicants for certain positions were required to show that they had had a number of years' office experience. Lately the regulations have been amended so as to dispense with that requirement where it can be shown that it is not necessary, and that the soldiers are sufficiently experienced in a broad way without requiring that specific number of years' office experience.
There may be a good deal in what the member for Calgary has said with regard to the commission giving proper notice and providing a proper length of time to enable soldiers to take advantage of the opportunity presented to them of getting a position.
As to the question of dependents, I would not like to say very much about that except to remark, in passing, that the dependent as ordinarily construed is one who is really a dependent; if he is able to earn a livelihood, in a sense he would no longer be a dependent. I assume what my hon. friend means that extra sympathy should be shown and attention given to those who are near relatives to soldiers who have seen service.
Mr. REDMAlN: When a man receives a pension it means that he has lost certain means of support.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
At all events, that will have full attention and sympathy.
The member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) spoke of examinations and rather deprecated the holding of examinations for technical positions. I can understand the difficulties that might be encountered in that respect. If, for instance, a returned soldier wanted a position in mining, geological or entomological work, it is quite obvious that technical knowledge might be necessary in order to determine his usefulness in that line of work.
I should deprecate as much as the member for Calgary-the practice-I can understand it would arouse resentment if it were generally followed- of appointing young civilians to positions when it was possible to get returned soldiers who could anything like fill the positions. I doubt whether there are any cases where such civilians have been given the preference; where it has been done, the circumstances must have been very exceptional. Having regard to the enormous number of appointments
under consideration, I have no doubt that occasional mistakes are made, but I am sure that the Civil Service Commission are in sympathy with the principles laid down in this respect. For myself, I feel, as the House generally does, that no consideration is too great for those men who crossed the seas in order to fight in those days of peril for the perpetuation of our institutions. There have been cases-I am sure my hon. friend would be the last to deny it-where soldiers have been given positions who have made it very difficult for the authorities to retain them because of their having shown little aptitude or desire to do the work; and it has been naturally a painful business to dismiss them by virtue of the fact that they are returned soldiers. Yet in some cases it has been practically impossible to retain such a man because of the manner in which he did the work. On the other hand, employers generally and the public should have the strongest and most abundant sympathy for men who have been wounded, especially, perhaps, for those who have been shell-shocked, and who having been given positions do the very best in them, but who cannot do as well as they might if they were restored to a normal state of health. The vast majority of men who have returned from the front whether wounded or unwounded-and one thinks more sympathetically of those who have been wounded -after facing the stark realities of life and death over there during three or more grim years of war, will not only be bigger men all round, but will, in the long run, do better than ever before in whatever particular class of work they were formerly engaged.
I do not suppose that the mover of the resolution intends to press it to a vote, because the Civil Service Act is going to be amended. Amendments will be brought down within the next few weeks, when these and other points may very well be taken up. In the meantime the attention of the Civil Service Commissioners will be directed to the motion of my hon. friend and to the discussion that has taken place on it. When the amendments are brought down opportunities will be afforded to the mover of the resolution, and to those who have spoken, to press the points on which they have touched.
Mr. W. F, NICKLE (Kingston): Before the member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) takes advantage of his right to close this debate or decides whether or not he will withdraw his resolution, I should like to

make a few remarks on the matter under discussion.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion this afternoon, more particularly to the remarks of the minister (Hon. Mr. Burrell). When he said that the matter would be taken into sympathetic consideration, he reminded me of a story I read some years ago of a colonel, who, passing down the Strand in London, saw a private of his regiment selling mutton pies by the street side. He stopped and spoke to him, and discovering the condition in which the man was, said: " You have my deepest sympathy"; to which the man replied: " Darn your sympathy; buy a pie." It is not sympathy that the returned soldier wants or that those of us who are speaking this afternoon on his behalf, desire. What he wants is recognition by way of appointment, recognition in the Civil Service, recognition throughout the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext: I hope my hon. friend is not arguing that I offered plain sympathy without asserting any intention of doing anything in a practical way, for such is not the case.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Is not that exactly what the Civil Service Commission are doing ?
Mr. N'ICKLE:	If my hon. friend will
allow me to proceed I will explain my position in a few moments. The net result of paragraph (a) was this: That where the minimum number of marks was obtained, the soldier should go to the top. But, in part, the difficulties arising at the present time are in connection with professional or technical positions, which, as the hon. member for Calgary states are filled without an examination being held. In that class of cases the Commission have no such regard for what I might call the preferential treatment set out in paragraph (a) of section 39, or by section 45 which established a principle that was not recognized when patronage .was in the control of private members. Then, promotion was not an essential of recognization:	it
was a question of selection, and not necessarily of promotion. But section 45 provided that :
Vacancies shall be filled, as far as is consistent with the best interests of the Civil Service, by promotion.
To put the matter briefly it comes down to this. Where there is an examination, either competitive or otherwise, marks being the determining factor, the returned successful soldier goes to the top of the list, but where it is a question of technical or professional qualification, the Civil 'Service Act makes no provision for such recognition of the returned or disabled soldier; and where it is a question of promotion, no recognition is given to the returned soldier as such.	>
Recently I have received from three organizations in my riding three resolutions. The first is a resolution passed on the 11th day of March by the Great War Veterans' Association, and reads as follows:
That this association, is of the opinion that the present practice of the Civil Service Commission in not carrying out its avowed policy in dealing with returned men deserves strong condemnation.
Another resolution was passed by the Soldiers' Aid Commission for the city of Kingston, and as you know, Mr. Speaker, the Soldiers' Aid Commission is organized for the express purpose of aiding and obtaining employment for the returned soldier. This resolution reads:
That this branch of the Soldiers' Aid Commission of the province of Ontario should go on reoord as favouring a change in the existing regulations of the Civil Service Commission, making it possible for returned men to secure government positions and appointments with the least possible amount of difficulty, haying due regard for the efficiency of the service; that every opportunity should be given at all times for the returned soldier to qualify for Civil Service positions, and that in the filling of positions rendered vacant by any cause, a returned soldier, all other things being equal, shall have the preference, and shall be given every chance to qualify.
'The Army and Navy Veterans' Association also passed a resolution unanimously supporting the resolution as moved in this House this afternoon by the hon. member for Colchester (IMr. McCurdy).
The hon. member for North iPerth (Mr. Morphy) asked me a question a few moments ago, and it was a very, very pertinent question and merits, I think, a careful answer, and I want for the edification of the House as well as of the hon. member to read two sets of letters which I think will make clear that the Civil Service Commission, while they may be endeavouring-to give them every credit-to carry out the principles of the Civil Service Act-are through the details of the regulations and the restriction of sections 15 and 45, not able to implement as fully as the House would desire the rights of the returned soldiers. In reading these letters, I do not intend to give the names of the soldiers mentioned therein. One letter dated December 23, 1918, was written by myself to the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission, Ottawa:-
Kingston, Ontario, December 23rd, 1918.
Chairman,
Civil Service Commission,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Roche:
Mr. X. of this city went overseas as a member of the C.E.F. and had the misfortune to

lose his right arm close to the shoulder. Prior to going overseas, he had had excellent experience in his father's factory and is thoroughly conversant with the management of men, general manufacturing, and ordinary commercial bookkeeping work and methods. He now desires to devote his energies to something that offers a prospect of advancement. I suggested some position akin to that of assistant postmaster, assistant collector of customs, or other work requiring honesty, energy and application. I wish you would send me the necessary form of application and also advise me if you know of any vacancy. I can speak in the highest terms of the young rnan who expects shortly to return to England to be married, and is therefore anxious to know something definite in regard to his future.
To which I received the following reply, dated December 27th:-
December 27, 1918.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge yours of the 23rd on behalf of Mr. X.
I am enclosing you a form of application for temporary employment which Mr. X. might fill in and return to -the Commission, so that we may have his name on file in the event of temporary help being requisitioned for by any of the departments in the line for which Mr, X.'s qualifications would fit him.
As you are aware, under the Civil Service Act 1918, all clerical positions of a permanent character must he filled after passing the regular Civil Service examination. We will have a large list of eligibles as a result of our examinations held on the 13th instant. There are other positions, however, of a special or technical character that you no doubt see advertized in the Canada Gazette from time to time and which advertisements are copied into the press of the country and are also sent to public institutions and to all the branches of the Great War Veterans' Associations, etc., which positions do not require the passing of the regular academic examination but are thrown open to public competition and selections are made on merit, returned soldiers of course being given the preference, all other things being equal.
The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) will now realize why I did not answer his question at the moment he asked it. That letter of the Civil Service Commission stipulates a provision that is very detrimental to the returned soldier, namely, that if he has not passed the examination held at the regular period he is prevented from recognition until another examination is held. And as these examinations are held only every two or three months, or, perhaps, every five or six months, the man who came back on the 27th of December, 1918, according to the terms of that letter in so far as I have read it-and I purpose to read it to the end, was denied recognition at least until the next examination was held. Now I shall proceed with the letter:
There is at the present time no request before the Commission to fill such position's as you have mentioned, namely assistant post-

master, assistant collector of customs, etc., but such positions are filled by promotion if there is any person on the staff qualified to fill same. If new appointments of this nature are required to be made, open competition is invited.
The letter is concluded in the formal manner.
As regards recognition by promotion, the gentleman on whose behalf I wrote had no chance Whatever unless he began at the bottom, no matter what his capabilities were. Because he had given up a position of ease and affluence and gone to the war, in which he lost an arm, he was in an infinitely more disadvantageous position than the man who remained at home and held his position in the Civil Service. The latter receives promotion, whereas the man who went overseas, was injured and could not resume his former employment, would be obliged to start at the bottom with $500 or $600 a year. The man who' stayed at home is promoted to a position that is worth $2,000 or $2,500 a year.
Hon, Mr. MACLEAN: Suppose he were an elderly man who could not go overseas, and who could not be expected to do so, should he not be given promotion?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I will say frankly that I think each case must be considered on its merits in relatinn to the situation that exists at the time. If the man who holds a position in the Civil .Service is an aged man with a family, and has given honest and faithful service, while the man desiring recognition is a young man, I think in all fairness the elderly man should get the preference, and if possible the younger man be given the position next vacant. But if a young man holds an important position won by ability and application, and the man returned from overseas is married and has two or three children, the recognition should he given to the man who has been to the front. Underlying this, the broad principle should be that the returned man, particularly if he is capable, should be regarded with singular care and sympathy by this House, by the Government and by the commission. I shall now read another letter writen by me on March 17, 1919, to the Civil Service Commission.
Kingston, Ontario,
March 17, 1919.
The Civil Service Commission,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sirs:-Mr. Y. now lives at X. street, having returned from the front where he went in ,1916. For eight months he was laid up with a broken leg and an injured neck as the result of concussion hut is now quite himself again.

He desires to be appointed as letter carrier and appears to have all the qualifications that that position would require. As he is married,-his wife and children living here with him-he would prefer an appointment to the Kingston staff, if an opportunity offers but would, if such were not available, go elsewhere. He tells me he sent in an application through the Postmaster over a month ago but has heard nothing in reference to the matter.
Please be good enough to see this letter is filed for reference.
Yours sincerely,
W. P. Niokle.
On March 20, I received this reply:
Ottawa, March 20, 1919.
Dear Sir:
I have your letter of the 17th instant, respecting- the case of Mr. Y., a returned soldier, who desires a position as Letter Carrier, if possible in Kingston Post Office. I am sending Mr. Y. an application form asking him to fill out and return it at his convenience. I may add, however, that vacancies are filled as far as possible from the lists of successful candidates at the regular examinations. When these lists are exhausted, however, other applications are considered and I can assure you that Mr. Y's case will be given every attention.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) W. Foran,
Secretary.
Mr. W. F. Nickle, Esq. M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
The net result is that, attaching so much importance to academic- qualifications as demonstrated by examinations the returned soldier, if he is here, and successful may go to the top of the list. We are demobilizing men at the rate of 30,000 or 40,000 a month, and these men are not in a position to get recognition in examinations until the regular examination is held. The provision is also made by the Civil Service Act subsection 5 of section 39:
If there remain from a previous examination successful competitors who have not received appointments, their number shall be deducted in making the computation, and their 'names, in the order of merit, shall be placed at the top of the list to be prepared in accordance with subsection 2 of this section.
In other words if all the positions have been filled and there are ten or twelve civilians unappointed after the first examination,' should the Civil Service Commission decide to have a second examination those civilians who were successful at the first examination take priority, although soldiers may have passed in the second examination. I do not believe this was the purport of the legislation passed last session, and the Act should be amended to carry out what was undoubtedly the principle that moved this House, namely that the returned man, particularly when disabled, should be given the preference. Now in regard to the point taken in one of these letters; " all other things being equal," I remember once having heard a shepherd remark that no two sheep were alike, and that he could distinguish each by its face. I think the same thing holds true with men; no two men are exactly alike, neither have they exactly the same qualifications. The difference between some men are remarkable, and between others, trifling. But there is always a difference. If the principle is going to be laid down that the returned soldier shall get the preference only when all other things are equal, it practically means that he will be given no preference at all; because it is only when two men are equally qualified and equally entitled to a position that the returned soldier gets the preference. That nicety of selection simply means that the recognition of priority for the soldier is destroyed. I think there is a tendency to attach too much importance to academic qualifications as demonstrated by marks obtained in examinations. The academic qualification is valuable in that it indicates training and intellectual status.
Academic qualifications are all right as far as they indicate training and intellectual status but they are not all right when you attach so much importance to them that you forget what one might call aptitude, ability and resourcefulness. In the soldier's case the experience that he has had overseas will, in my judgment, in many cases, make him a better man than before he went. I believe that a man who went overseas three or four years ago and who, actively guided by a strong sense of patriotism and a consciousness that he was doing his duty, stood to his post and did his bit as a true soldier has qualifications that you cannot measure by an academic test, and which you cannot judge by his capacity to stand high in an examination in long division or in extracting the cubic root. I would not say that examinations must not be held. I admit that you must test a man's worth in some way and an academic examination is one sort of a test but I would like to see the working out of the Act so changed that when an appointment came up the list that was secured four or five weeks or perhaps seven or eight or perhaps months ago, would not be taken as the list from which the appointment would be made. I believe that some steps should be taken to find out if there were any returned men available who could do this work, even though those men had not made application, and if it was found on inquiry that such a man existed,

an opportunity should be given him to demonstrate his worth and, if he satisfied the commission, not necessarily by an academic examination, of his capacity to undertake the job, he should be given the position regardless of the fact that he did not have an opportunity of writing on an examination which was held in the regular course of events
I think this demand is going to grow in so far as the Civil Service is concerned -I was going to say worse and worse- but I will change that and say steadily. Men are coming back from the front and their disability claims are rapidly being adjusted by the Pension Commissioners. I suppose we will have, when we have got through, 60,000 disabled men. These are men whose earning capacity is impaired through service and the question is: Where are these men going to get employment and what is going to be the policy of the country, both from the point of view of the Government and from the point of view of the captains of industry, as to what use we are going to make of the residuum of ability that these men have?
The House will remember that pensions are not voted by way of compensation. They are not voted with respect to a man's pre-war earnings; nor are they voted with respect to his impairment in relation to his pre-war occupation. A pension is voted to a man with reference to the amount of work which it may be determined he may be able to do in the ordinary unskilled labour market of the world. The result is that many men of high technical qualifications, education and broad experience are finding themselves impaired in relation to their pre-war occupations and are unable to live adequately on the pensions that have been or will be, granted to them.
As these men, driven from their pre-war occupations, go about this country seeking new occupations, they are confronted, and are apt to be confronted more and more, with this problem that the employer has to solve: Am I justified, in relation to the Workmen's Compensation Act, under which I am now called upon to make compensation, to those of my employees who are hurt, in taking these men back again into my employ? What risk do I incur if I take back into my employment a man who is disabled .as a result of service?
The reason I allude to that point is this: The pressure under the Civil Service Act and the pressure from the country for recognition by the employment of returned men is going to depend largely on how far 
these returned men may or can be absorbed into the industrial, commercial and agricultural life of the community. The principles that underlie the Compensation Act fall into two classes. Some of the compensation acts are worked out on the principle of assessment and others on the principle of individual responsibility. Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, to an extent Manitoba, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have worked out their compensation acts on the principle of assessment. The industries of the different districts 'are divided into thirty-five or forty classes. The hazard of each is determined and a rate struck. That rate is levied on the average wage paid during the year. In some cases it runs as low as ten cents on the $100 and in others it goes as high as $4 or $5 to each $100 of wages paid during the year. The average is about one per cent of the wages paid. In Quebec and in other provinces the assessment system does not prevail. The employer is responsible for the compensation to be paid to the employee. Each factory bears its own losses, and the manufacturer is deprived of the right of setting up the old common law defence of contributory negligence and voluntary incurment of risk. These principles are set to one side and if an accident happens the employer must pay the man who is regarded, so to .speak, as a part of the -machinery of the factory, and if a part of the machinery is injured the responsibility for compensation is thrown on the owner of the industry. There is no escaping the obligation. That obligation, in those provinces in which individual responsibility prevails, is largely met by the manufacturers carrying insurance in some of the line companies that carry on that class of insurance. You can readily see from this that the problem which confronts the employer coming under either of the two systems is if he takes back the returned man and the compensation for disability is increased. If this happens to be 'an employment in which many men are engaged, consideration is not so important as in the smaller employments where a few men are engaged. If only two or three are engaged the responsibility will make a tremendous increase in the risk. I am quite willing to admit that the great majority of the employers of this country are patriotic. I am quite willing to admit that the great majority of employers are anxious to take back into their employment men who left them to go overseas. They are anxious in so far as they can, to give

employment to the men who have returned and are looking for work although, when they went overseas they may not have been employed in the particular factory of the employer, who is asked to take them on. But, we must follow that out and find where we are being led. There is no question-it cannot be disputed-that where a man has suffered any disability he will be more awkward and less alert than the man who has not suffered such a disability. Working about rapidly moving machinery which is the very backbone of industry to-day, that man may not find his senses as keen and cannot respond as rapidly to the premonitions of danger as the man who has his full faculties about him. The restrictions under which he works tend to increase accidents. If, these accidents do increase, as accidents are bound to increase I think that the dollar and cents argument will be likely to prevail. The economic argument will be felt' that each man must endeavour to conduct his factory on a basis to enable him to compete with those who are not as patriotic as himself. As that argument begins to be felt, or as that pressure begins to be felt, there will arise a tendency not to keep the returned man in the employ of this industry or that. Now I had a very striking instance of that a few months ago. There is in my riding a shipbuilding company who are anxious, and have always been glad, to give the returned man recognition. A returned man came into my office and told me he could not get work. I asked the shipbuilding company would they take him on, and they said, "Send him down," and they gave him work. He had not worked there more than a few weeks, when one day, whilst walking across a narrow bridge, he had a fit of dizziness, fell off the bridge and was drowned, with the result that I believe some four or five thousand dollars has been, or will have to be, paid to his dependents. That claim is going to be thrown on the shipbuilding industry. Naturally that industry would likely say, "We do not want to take on any more men like that if we have got to meet the cost incidental to such an accident." Then there is another class of cases, a very serious class, where a man has had a disability that leaves him a fair residuum of ability to carry on his ordinary work in life. We will take a man who has lost one eye, but whose other eye is perfectly good. One eye is fairly capable of doing the work that the man has to do, working about machinery, or working out of doors; but if he loses the second eye that man becomes 63
stone blind and cannot carry on his work.
A man has lost two fingers off his right hand. He is quite capable of doing his work, and doing his work well, but if in addition to the two fingers he loses two more, and loses his thumb, his whole hand is gone. Now what is to be the principle that is to underlie the recognition that is to be given under the Workmen's Compensation Act, where a man suffers an impairment, subsequent to his war disability, on going into industrial employment? Is the workman's compensation to be on the basis of the injury the man suffered through his industrial activity without relation to his war disability, or is the compensation to be determined, by the disability the man suffers in relation to his condition on the assumption that he was a whole man when he went into that employment?
Then there is another class of cases. A man comes back from the front. He has been away from the industry two or three years. He is not as skilled a man as he was when he went away. He has lost the skill that comes from long unbroken practice. He has suffered some injury at the front, say a wound that is fully healed, and he comes back into industry. While he is working along, being a bit clumsy, he gets struck right on the old wound, and the old war disability returns, and instead of taking two or three weeks it takes him five or six months to get better. Is his compensation going to be paid in respect of two or three weeks, or in respect of five or six months?	.
You ask me what are my-suggestions for these difficulties and why do I bring them up this afternoon? As I told you I bring them up because I believe they have to be met. Primarily, I bring them up because I believe if they are not met we are going to have so many men looking for Government recognition in this country by virtue of Civil Service appointments that Governments are going to be decidedly uncomfortable. You have a right to say to me" You are criticizing, do some constructing. A man of very moderate ability can be a very hitter critic; it takes a good man to be a passable performer." You have a right to ask me to become a passable performer; and I want to submit to the House a few suggeptions which I think 'it should take into its consideration. The United States, Italy, France and Great Britain have had this matter under review. They have realized that the returned man has a right to his place in the community. He has a right to his citizenship, and I mean by the



expression he has a right to his citizenship, that he has a right if he desires it when he comes back to this country to be given some employment in. which he will have a reasonable opportunity of earning his daily bread, and that he should not be made to feel in this country after having given, perhaps I might say, the best of his life, that there is no place in Canada for him, and that all he has ahead of him is to loaf the streets, living on a pittance of a pension; that there is no place in Canada where he can turn the ability he may have left to account and do something to advance the interests of his family. Nothing is worse than that. I do not sympathize with those that believe that work is a burden. I believe that work, honest work, in reason, is the salvation of mankind; and I believe that honest work for the returned soldier is going to be the very best thing that this country can offer him. Of course a pension, with respect to his disability, as well with honest work for the returned soldier is going to be the best thing that this country can offer to him if we are in the years to come to have a contented, thrifty and satisfied class in Canada, among those whom we call the returned men.
Now, the suggestion I make is this, and I divide it into three classes, because I have not had sufficient opportunity to reach a conclusion-I have not been able to get sufficient information to warrant me in finally saying what I think should be done: As I have endeavoured to explain to the House, Sir, the Workmen's Compensation Acts, all proceed on the assumption that the disabled man in industry shall get something in respect of his industrial disability. To give that compensation means that industry, as a class, or individual employers, must meet the cost. Shifting the burden of taxation does not pay the taxes. Shifting the burden incidental to the risk of employment from one industry to a 5 p.m. group of industries does not pay the compensation incidental to the occupation, it simply shifts it, so to speak, in that it equalizes the burden over the entire industry and takes it off a particular shop. I would like to suggest to the Governme'nt, therefore, that they should carefully consider this point-that they should insure all returned men as against industrial disability. This would create of the returned men a preferred class, because the manufacturers of this country would be brought to realize that the returned men put no burden on them in respect of workmen's compensation. If they took a man 
into a particular industry and an accident happened to him, the state would bear the loss, the industry would be spared that loss, and the amount, in my judgment, would not be so excessive. I believe you could dO' it at a cost of a million dollars a year, and I do not believe it should be done-at least at the beginning it should not be held out that it would be done-for more than five years, and I think the principle should not aipply to men who had not been in the army, let us say, six months or a year. Now the reason I say that the man should be in the army at least six months or a year is this: Some men were drafted into the army and were only in it a few weeks. Other men volunteered and were only in a few weeks. Some men are coming back and are going back into civil life exactly as well as when they left it, because they were not in the army long enough to be physically impaired. Others have been as I have endeavoured to show, long enough in the army to be seriously impaired, and these are the men that I think should be protected. I want to be frank with the House: In making this suggestion I am making a suggestion that will, to a certain extent, be beneficial to the employer, and will be beneficial for this reason: In all classes of industry certain men are injured, not through any negligence of the men, not through any negligence-as the law would determine negligence,-of the employer, but by what I would call unavoidable accident. A boiler may explode, a wall may fall, something of that sort may happen, by which returned men would be injured, and yet their injury would in no way be attributable to any disability they might have incurred during the war. Some people may say, "That is too broad a scheme, it is too big a scheme, the Government should not commit itself to it." If they cannot do that, insure all pensionable disabled men- as against industrial disability, who have been recognized by their being pensioned, are suffering from disability due to the fact that they have been impaired, and permanently impaired through service, or during service.
As far as I can estimate it, there will probably be 60,000 of those men, of whom about two-fifths will go into industrial or commercial pursuits. As I saici some little time ago Sir, the average protection rate is about one per cent, and it has been computed that it costs on the average about $7 a year to insure a man against industrial disability. Two-fifths of 60,000 will give us

24,000, and at $7 a man that would involve an annual expenditure of $168,000. That is all it would cost this country to insure the pensionable disabled man, and in that way I think we would guarantee them employment in the industries of this country.
But if you are not prepared to do that, then let us at least think of this, which although not nearly enough, is something that the returned man is entitled to be given .insurance against, the increased liability to industrial accidents due to his disability.
If the loss of one eye is valued at 30 per cent by the Pension Board, and by the Workmen's Compensation Board, then when a man loses one eye during service he will be given a pension of 30 per cent, and if he loses the other eye, becoming totally blind, the industrial compensation being only another 30 per cent, then the man who has become stone blind in industrial service will only get 60 per cent, unless the aggravated disability of 70 per cent is charged against industry by the Compensation Board. Surely that man is entitled' to a hundred per cent disability. If the Government is not prepared to adopt either of the first two schemes, surely the suggestion I make in regard to insurance against increased liability for aggravation from industrial accidents is something that this country should and likely will be willing to undertake.
It is a responsibility which should not be shifted on to the employers. I recognize their patriotism, their anxiety to do everything they can to give employment to returned men, but I know how inexorable the laws of supply and demand are, how inexorably the law of costs bears down on industry, and if a manufacturer finds that by reason of keen competition he is making a loss, as sure as the sun rises in the morning, he is going to cut down his costs, and the only way he can do so is by increasing his efficiency, by stripping his factory of every overhead charge that can be eliminated, and I am afraid that in the years to come one of the first to suffer will be the disabled man.
You may say that much of what I have advanced has nothing to do with the Civil Service Commission. I think it has a great deal to do with the Civil Service Commission. because I appreciate the problems with which they have to deal. I appreciate that there is much discontent among our returned men at the present time, and I agree with what the hon. member for Calgary said, that there is one thing that the returned man resents, and that is a young man getting recognition, and I know as I
63*
speak on the floor of this House that, unless a change has taken place in the last few weeks, there is one young man in Kingston holding a Government position that should be given to a returned man, and he is holding that position because somebody more powerful than the member wants to keep him there. It is now only a temporary position, but it is a temporary position that has been held for a period of from eighteen months to two years, and just as sure as I stand on this floor to-night 1 am confident that the reason that young man is being kept in that temporary position is that it is desired that some day his appointment be made permanent. I ask the minister and this House: Is there any reason why an able bodied young man who has not been at the front should not give way, even although he is a temporary employee of this Government, to the returned man who has lost an eye or an arm or a leg in the service of his country, but has all the other qualifications essential to fill that position? I do not think that this country wants the retention of these positions by men who are physically fit, and I want to urge that on the Civil Service Commission. As I said before, I am in favour of the Civil Service Commission, I do not want the worry and anxiety of political patronage, but if the Civil Service Commission is going to continue, both the commission and this Government have got to be alive to the fact that public sentiment from one end of this country to the other demands that full and generous recognition be given to the returned men; and the people of this country are determined that the returned men shall not be deprived of the recognition they are entitled to merely for technical and trivial reasons.

Will the hon. gentleman

Mr. N'JCKLE: I think I drew the attention of the Civil Service Commission to the fact.
