speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the resolution before the House touches a real live question, a

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, The subject under discussion I conceive to be one of the most important that will be touched upon this session, and the member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) is entitled to credit for bringing the resolution before the House.
While I agree with the resolution and the spirit of it, I cannot believe that it is broad enough to suit the exigencies of the situation in Canada to-day. The resolution reads :
That, in the opinion of this House, the Civil Service Act should be amended so that, while having full regard, to efficiency, a preference in appointments to the public service shall be afforded to members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force who have become casualties in a theatre of war.
What I object to is that the resolution is narrowed down and restricted in its phraseology to apply only to casualties. The word 'casualty' is a very broad term, and as the resolution is now worded a man whose only injury was a sprained ankle or some minor flesh wound, who was in the trenches perhaps only one day before the fighting stopped, might get a preference over the man who had fought for his country for three or four years. I do not believe the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) intended so to restrict the meaning of his resolution. In fact, I have spoken to him about it, and he said he had no such intention; that his purpose was to get the matter before the House so that the House could settle on some one resolution.
I was rather surprised to learn to-day from the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) that the Civil Service Commission are not now giving a preference to returned soldiers. In correspondence which I have not here I have had word from the Civil

Service Commission directly to the contrary effect; they say that soldiers who have qualified at the examinations are being put at the top of the list. Now the Civil Service Commission is a creature of the Government, and I think it is about time that this Parliament should put forth an opinion that would have some effect upon the commission. Taking as true what the hon. member for Kingston has told the House to-day, I do not think there is a member of this House who would not condemn such a procedure being followed by the Civil Service Commission. According to the correspondence read, the commission are filling all the positions they can by examination, and now the hopper of applicants is absolutely congested, and the soldier who writes hereafter on an examination may not get a position for many years to come. Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is the spirit that actuates the Canadian people to-day; I do not think it is a practice that they will stand for. It is no use our crying out that we are going to do something for the soldier, and then by some pretence or specious practice have a Civil Service Commission doing everything to prevent the country doing something for the returned soldier. That is the only meaning I can see in the letters written to the hon. member for Kingston. I do not like the word "big stick;" I do not like using a club on anybody, hut I think a resolution that would influence the Civil Service Commission and would show the temper of the people of this country as reflected by the Canadian Parliament would be quite in order. And then, if the Government have any influence upon the Civil Service Commission-and T direct the attention of the Acting Prime Minister particularly to this -I would whisper into the ear of the chairman that he had better look alive to the welfare of the returned soldier and not play favourites in any other direction. To put the matter in what I conceive to be its proper position, and in order to make the resolution a little broader, while still preserving the spirit of the resolution of my hon. friend from Colchester, with his approval I am going to move in amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" in the original resolution be struck out and the . following substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this House the Civil Service Act should be amended so that priority in appointments to the public service shall after this date for one year be given to members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, Canadians in the Royal Air Force, and Canadians in the Imperial and allied armies who have served at the |front; disability, length of service and efficiency to be considered.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. W. WIGMORE (St, John City):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
In seconding this amendment I must say that I consider the resolution deals with one of the most important matters that have been discussed in this House since the opening of the session. I realize, as does every hon. member of this House and every citizen of Canada, that the returned soldiers feel that the Government is not keeping its pledges to the boys, that the promises which they made to the boys when they left for overseas were not sincere. I should just like to give a few concrete cases that have come under my observation in the constituency I represent, and I want first of all to say that the Great War Veterans' Association of the city of St. John are very much displeased indeed with the attitude of the Government. There have been a number of appointments made to positions in the city of St. John which returned soldiers could have filled just as efficiently as those who have been appointed. Not very long ago a letter-carrier was required in the post office department. Several returned soldiers applied, but unfortunately not one of them passed the necessary examination. That was how the Civil Service Commission got around it in that case. The result was that a boy of sixteen who, of course, had never served at the front was appointed to the position, and several returned soldiers were turned down. In another case a vacancy occurred in the Customs House. Several returned soldiers applied for the position, one of whom at least had passed the necessary preliminary examination. Another soldier, who had never been overseas but had been taken ill and placed in hospital at Ste. Agathe, was appointed because he had passed the qualifying examination whereas the other soldier had only passed the preliminary; and this appointment was made in the face of the recommendation of the Great War Veterans' Association and a number of prominent citizens of St. John. Similar cases are occurring every day, and the returned soldier is not at all satisfied with the treatment he is receiving.
In the Marine and Fisheries Department in the city of St. John a number of temporary vacancies occur that do not require examination. A very singular thing happened there not long ago. Dependents of soldiers overseas were dismissed while in some cases at least, men of military age and physically fit were retained.
One man had two sons overseas and another three, one of whom had been killed, and I think that in such cases preference should be given to the dependents of sol-

diers who have been overseas. Construction work is now in progress at Courtney Bay by the St. John Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Construction Company under sub-contract by the Bedford Construction Company. Scores of returned soldiers have applied for positions in connection with this work, but the preference has been nearly always given to civilians. This is a matter that the Government should endeavour to remedy.
I am entirely in favour of the amendment because I think the resolution does not go far enough. Preference should be given to the returned soldier in every case, and it should not be necessary in connection with appointments to positions such as that of watchman on a dock or of letter carrier to pass the rigid examinations which are required. I will support the amendment.

speechtext: As a matter of privilege I would ask that the words "and allied armies" be added after the words "Imperial army."

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I shall be brief in the expression of my opinion on this matter. In my judgment the resolution does not go far enough, and I shall support the amendment because it recognizes the military record and time service of our returned soldiers. Many applications have been made by returned soldiers for positions which I think they were qualified to fill, but their applications, for some reason or another, the Commission did not favourabley consider. Young men who were among the first to respond to the call, enlisting in the first week of the war, and who spent some winters in the trenches very much to the detriment of their health, have come back physically unfit, and when they apply for positions the Civil Service Commission inform them that they must have their discharge before their applications can be considered. Among the returned soldiers, many who have not lost limbs are suffering other disabilities which render them incapable of strenuous work, and it has often happened that men who were longest on active service and were discharged long ago have been put off, some who have not yet been discharged are urged to hurry up and get their discharge papers so that they may be appointed. Many a returned man who has won distinction on the field of battle is overlooked, and as I think that something should be done to remedy this condition of things, I shall support the amendment. I concur in the opinion that all appointments to the outside service for a year at least should
be reserved for discharged soldiers, and if in any county or parish there may not happen to be a soldier available to fill any vacant position, one from the adjoining county or parish might be selected..

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not desire to delay the House for any length of time, but coming from a constituency that sent a large number of its sons overseas, I feel it incumbent on me to say a few words on this question. We are indebted to the member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) for bringing so important a matter as this before us, and I wish to say, with all the emphasis I can, that the Goverement for some reason or other, are not doing what we expected they would do when the Civil Service Act was passed last year. I think I voice the opinion of members of the House as well as of returned soldiers and citizens generally when I say that too many of the returned men are being turned down in connection with appointments to the public service. This is a very serious matter and one that should be looked into by the proper authorities. There is a very deep-seated opinion current that things are not right and that the returned soldier is not being treated as he ought to be. He needs employment as soon as he is fit after his return, and if the policy that is outlined in the letter which was read this afternoon is one. that is being pursued by the Civil Service Commission, I can easily understand why dissatisfaction exists. The policy as iaid down in the letter read by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) is exactly contrary to what it should be. It is evidently the intention to exhaust the list of those civilians who have passed examinations before attention is given to the soldier. I would suggest that the proper course would be to consider the case of the returned soldier first, and let the civilians, no matter how high their marks may be, stand until the returned men have received their due.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: I have not the letter before me, but the practice is this: When an examination takes place those who are successful obtain recognition before the returned man who has not had an opportunity of passing the examination.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
That is quite as 1 understand it, and, as I say, is exactly contrary to what it should be. I think that these technical and academic examinations are entirely unnecessary -in the case of soldiers. If a soldier has sound common sense

and can fulfil the duties of the office to which he seeks appointment-and I would always qualify it in that way-he ought to have the first claim regardless of whether he can pass at the top of the list or not. He should be the first man to be considered, because the country owes him a duty which it can ill repay even if it gave him a very good position. In my opinion, therefore, the Civil Service Commission should seriously interest themselves in behalf of the returned soldiers and endeavour to place them in good positions as speedily as possible. It is quite true that members endeavoured to do that when they were dispensing the patronage. I received many circulars on that head and I always endeavoured to see that the returned soldier was the first man considered. In many cases no one else was considered. That is the way it should be before the Civil Service Commission.
I think the amendment of the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) is a very excellent one. I do not know how the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) may feel towards it. I think that Canadians who have enlisted in the air force, or in the marine, or in any of the Allied armies for that matter and have been wounded in battle or in the service of the country, are entitled to consideration. But whether it is the amendment that is put or whether it is the resolution, I want to go on record as being entirely in accord with the principle that is enunciated in both of them. I want to let it be distinctly understood that from now on the returned soldier gets the best of the deal all along the line and you cannot put that too strongly. He has not had it up to date to the extent that he should have had it. I would hold up both hands for giving all the positions to returned soldiers that they can fill. I would consider them first. Our duty is first to the soldier and after that the civilian list, which is a matter of very small importance, comparatively, may be considered. Before the soldiers are provided for, do not let any of these civilians in at all.

have listened with great attention to the remarks which have been made in reference to this question. I wish to place before the House the facts of a case that occurred in my own town. speechtext:
There is
one phase of this question that I would like to say a few words about and that has reference to the sending out of the advertisements to applicants seeking positions in the public service. In my own experience this advertisement comes along in western Canada too late for the applicant to get his application back to Ottawa in time to receive consideration at the hands of the Civil Service Commission. I do not know whether this is done intentionally or whether it is just carelessness on the part of the Commission. Through that practice alone there has been a tremendous injustice inflicted on all returned soldiers as well as on civilians who are looking for positions in the Civil Service. I am quite in accord with the sentiments expressed both by the mover of the resolution and the amendment.
I think the amendment moved by the honourable member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) is preferable to the resolution because it goes farther and I would therefore support it. Too little regard has been paid to the promises which have been made by the Government in regard to what shall be done for the returned soldiers and I hope that in the

future more consideration will be given to the promises and the pledges which were made to the men before they went overseas.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I
am in entire sympathy with the resolution and also with the amendment except that neither goes far enough. In neither is mention made of the Canadian navy or seamen of the mercantile marine. I would like to suggest to the honourable the mover of the amendment (Mr. Morphy) that the members of the Canadian navy and the seamen of the mercantile marine be also included. Whilst perhaps the Canadian navy did not get a chance to do very much during the war, the seamen of the merchant marine, during four years, were in every sea and faced the submarine danger. They are entitled to the sympathy of the Government just as much as the members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, the members of the Air Force of the Canadians who enlisted in the Imperial army.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: I would like to ask my hon. friend the mover of the amendment (Mr. Morphy) a question. The amendment says that disability, length of service and efficiency are to be considered. Is the proposal to make the Civil Service of Canada exclusive to returned men for one year, and is this consideration as to length of service, disability and efficiency to apply only among the returned men themselves and without regard to the efficiency of the Civil Service?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: I should say that they should be efficient to perform the duties.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: The resolution would not go to the extent of making the service exclusive for returned men without regard to the efficiency of the Civil Service of Canada?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: No, my intention is to put the returned soldier, if he is efficient, ahead of everybody else.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I have no hesitation whatever in supporting the resolution and the amendment as suggested. Campaigns have been carried on throughout the length and breadth of Canada asking employers to reinstate those men who left them when they enlisted for overseas service. Many men have been reinstated, but it has been found that they are unable to perform their duties to the same extent that they did when they went overseas, perhaps by reason of some nervous disability. The result has been that employers have discharged these men. But I think that the Dominion of Canada can take these men
into the Civil Service, and that even if they have not one hundred per cent efficiency in the performance of their duty there is no justification for their being discharged from the	Civil	Service on
the same ground that they would be discharged from private employment.
When we take a large manufacturing industry, or some mercantile business, we know that throughout the length and breadth of the country the competition is. very keen. An employer may be very good hearted and may desire to retain all these men, but he finds that he is up against the competition of those engaged in the same business, and that he cannot successfully carry on his activities, or successfully compete with his rivals if he yields to good nature.
I think the resolution which has been brought in by the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) covers that class of cases. I also think that provision should be made in the Civil Service of the country for those men who are casualties, or who are suffering from physical or nervous defects which prevent them from carrying on their duties as they did before they went to the front. We owe a duty to these men to see that they are provided for, and that they have the same source of income and maintenance as they did when they were engaged in industrial pursuits. I have very much pleasure in supporting the resolution as introduced by the hon. member for Colchester, and also the amendment, due regard being paid to the necessity of the maintenance of efficiency in the Civil Service. I also wish to support the stand taken by some hon. gentlemen with regard to that service. I think it would be very unfortunate for Canada if, for any reason, we should abandon the reform which we adopted last year and returned to the old system of party patronage which previously prevailed in this country.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Both the resolution and the amendment have evidently met with a very substantial and favourable response in the House. I would like, however, to suggest that when it is proposed to make amendments to the Civil Service Act of the nature proposed it would be well if the opportunity were afforded of giving very careful consideration to the details of such amendments. In the course of two or three weeks very important and substantial amendments to the Civil Service Act will be submitted to Parliament, and I would suggest for the consideration of the mover of the resolution, and of

the mover of the amendment as well, the desirability of postponing until then consideration of the proposals set forth today. Every opportunity will he afforded the members of the House to submit amendments of this character when the Bill is introduced, and in the meantime I can assure both hon. gentleman that the Government will give every consideration to the proposals which have been presented to-day. I trust that both hon. gentlemen will refrain from asking for a formal adoption of their proposals upon my assuring them that the Government will take careful cognizance of the matters which have been referred to, and that in the course of two or three weeks, or a month at the least, there will be ample opportunity of considering amendments of this nature to the Civil Service Act.

I might request the privilege of adding that he will hasten down to the Civil Service Commission in the morning and put a flea in the ear of the authorities there so that they may keep moving in accordance with the spirit of the House as evidenced by what has taken place here to-day.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext:
Mr. WILLIAM D. EULER (Waterloo North) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, all Ministers of the Crown should be members of the House of Commons, or become such within a period of three months after their appointment to the Cabinet.
He said: Mr. Speaker, after the strenuous debates of last week, and which developed acute differences of opinion among honourable members, I propose a resolution this evening that I believe should be, in principle, acceptable to a very large majojity of the members of the House-that is, providing that the Government do not make it a party question. And I think, Sir, that it is not a party question because the practice of appointing senators to the Cabinet of Canada, as is well known, is one which has been followed by both Liberal and Conservative Governments in the past.
Last week in connection with the debate on daylight saving, I was pleased to note the action of the Government, in that they appeared to give a certain freedom of speech and of action to hon. members on their side of the House. I rather suspect that the reason for that action was because the Government did not care to assume the responsibility of re-enacting that measure;

but be that as it may, I am willing to give the Government the benefit of the doubt, because I believe that it is in the interest of Parliament that there should be permitted to the hon. members on the opposite side of the House a reasonable independence of action, rather than that the majority in this House should resolve itself merely into a rubber stamp to record the wishes of the Cabinet.
I am certain, Mr. Speaker, that the significance of the resolution which I propose is quite evident to every hon. member.
If I were speaking in a general way, I should say that it is intended as a step towards a more advanced and complete democracy. And when I use the word " democracy," Mr. Speaker, I realize that in the last few years it has become somewhat hackneyed and that perhaps to most of us it is more a matter of sound than of meaning. The hon. member for South York (Mr. W. P. Maclean), in the debate on daylight saving last week, made a statement that during the course of the war, and especially in the last year or so, the Government had found it necessary to suspend in some degree the principle of responsible government. I do not agree with him when he says that it was necessary even then; but I do agree with him that the time has arrived when responsible government in full measure ought to be restored. If it is indeed true that the war which has just ended was a war " to make the world safe for democracy," then, Sir, I contend we ought to use every opportunity to carry into effect in a concrete way the principles that we were fighting for. We should not be afraid to take our own medicine, but should let democracy, like charity, begin at home.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, the resolution which I have offered has for its object the debarring from the Cabinet of members of the Senate, for what I consider to be the sufficient reason, that members of the Senate, not being elected, are not representative of, and not responsible to, the people. I am quite prepared to have some hon. gentlemen say that the easiest way to accomplish that which is desired in the resolution would be to abolish the Senate entirely, and if any hon. members choose to offer a Bill in that regard, I for one would support it. I have not risen this evening with any intention of dealing with the Senate as a body, but it does appear to me that in these so-called democratic times a non-elective Senate is something of an anomaly in this country.
We have been told, Sir, that the Senate is established more to protect minorities than perhaps anything else. I do not think that the history of Canada shows that they have had any very great success in that direction. In fact, it seems to me that at the present day the Senate is more in the public eye, because by force of circumstances it has become established as something of a clearing house for the obligations of those who desire to free themselves from the bonds of matrimony -it has become something of a divorce court. But in order to abolish the Senate constitutional action would be necessary; to follow out that which I propose would require no change whatever in the Constitution, the British North America Act, and if this House saw fit to pass this resolution, it could easily be carried into concrete effect simply by the Government adopting the principle upon which the House placed itself on record.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as is well known, senators are not elected. They are merely the partisan appointees of the Prime Minister or of the political party which happens to be in power. That, I submit. Sir, is not by any means an indication that the men so appointed possess the confidence of the country. Indeed it is only too true that exactly the reverse is the case in very many instances, and that men who have been rejected when they have offered themselves for election to the House of Commons are frequently appointed to the Senate merely as a reward for party service.
The responsibility and power of the ministry are very great. During the past two years the power of the Cabinet has been greater even than the power of Parliament itself. That was during the war. As a matter of fact, the War Measures Act is still in force and the Government still retains that power. But even after the War Measures Act becomes null and void the power and influence of the Cabinet will still remain very great. Members of the Cabinet who are of sufficient calibre to deserve a position as responsible as that, wield a tremendous power not only in the formulating of policies, but also in the administration of the departments over which they have control.
The appointment of senators to the Dominion Cabinet is entirely subversive of the principle of responsible government.
I bring this matter before the House at this time because I feel that the abuse I think it is an abuse-to which I refer appears to be growing. We have in the Cabinet at the present time no fewer than three

members of the Senate; more, I think, than we have ever had since we first enjoyed responsible government. First of all, we have the leader of the Senate (Sir James Loug-heed), who is Minister of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. This afternoon we had a very interesting and lengthy debate on the matter of the appointment of soldiers to positions in the Civil Service, and we shall have a great deal of that this year and in the years to come. It seems to me that a minister holding the important portfolio of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment should be present on the floor of this House to give his advice to members and to answer questions that may be put from time to time.
The same is true of the Minister of Labour, Hon. G. D. Robertson, who also is a member of the Senate and has not a seat in this House. One of the most difficult and important questions with which this country will have to deal in the future is the question of labour, therefore this Parliament will necessarily have to concern itself with legislation affecting labour. Old age pensions, pensions to widows, and legislation on matters of labour will have to be considered by this House in the very near future. I do not think that the Government is doing its duty to the people, particularly to the working men, in not having in this House, as head of the Department of Labour, a man who manifestly, by election, enjoys the confidence of the people whom he is supposed to represent.
Then I come to what everybody must consider the most glaring instance of the violation of the principles of responsible government that one could possibly conceive. And, by the way, I make these criticisms not at all in a personal sense, but only in so far as they affect the public service and the public good. We have as Postmaster General Hon. P. E. Blondin, a member of the Senate, a gentleman who in the elections of 1917 offered himself for election in two constituencies and was overwhelmingly defeated in both; in one by a majority of about 1,200 votes and in the other by a majority of no less than 6,500 votes, receiving himself only 500 votes in the constituency of 'Champlain. This gentleman is in charge of a department which employs about 10,000 persons, which has in its control the expenditure of something like $18,000,000 a year. Yet, in the face of the fact that this gentleman was rejected by his constituents; in face of the very evident fact that he does not possess the confidence of the electors of Canada, the Prime Minister has retained him in an office which, it will not 
be denied, should not be occupied by any one who is not responsible to the people and who does not occupy a seat in the House of Commons. The 'Postmaster General is not answerable to Parliament; the same may be said of all members of the Senate who hold portfolios in the Cabinet. They are not on the floor of the House to answer questions or to pass their own estimates through Parliament.
We were told this afternoon in a return that the Postmaster General is represented in this House by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). I do not know whether that gentleman has informed himself very particularly as to the details of the Post Office Department; I doubt it very much. At the same time, most of us are willing to admit that the duties of the President of the Privy Council are so light that possibly he feels that the large honorarium that he receives may very well justify his giving some attention to the work of the Postmaster General. But I do contend that the appointment of three members of the Senate to positions in the ministry is the very negation of responsible government. In the case of the office of the Postmaster General it is nothing less than an arrogant defiance of the will of the people which this Parliament, if it dares to call its soul its own, should not tolerate any longer.
If any reply is made to the arguments that I offer, the first may be that Liberal Governments in the past have appointed Senators to the Cabinet. That is true, although I do not think that it is true in such a glaring degree as it is in the case of the office of Postmaster General. But even if it be true, I do not for one moment admit that that affects the argument in the slightest degree. That a Liberal Government did what has been done by a Unionist or Conservative Government makes it neither right nor wrong; the question should be decided entirely upon its merits.
It may also be stated that a similar practice is followed in the British Government; that members of the House of Lords occupy portfolios in tire British Cabinet. That also is true, and while I admit that we have taken from the British practice and the British. Constitution many desirable things and incorporated them into our own system of government, it does not follow that we must in every respect follow the example of England. Our conditions and political development have been in many respects entirely different from those of Great Britain. The British have travelled a very

long way through all the stages of feudalism, autocracy and rule by the aristocracy, and while they have made great progress on the way to democracy I.do not think that the most ardent Britisher would claim that they have yet attained to the very highest ideals of democracy and that no further progress is possible for them. But even if that were contended, again I would ' say that the mere fact that a thing is good in England does not necessarily make it good in Canada. Moreover, in England when a member of the House of Lords "holds a portfolio in the Cabinet, in almost all cases the department over which he presides is represented in the House of Commons by an under-secretary.
The constitution of Canada never contemplated that a member of the Senate should be appointed to the responsible position of Minister of the Crown. That is quite apparent when we consider that when a member of the House of Commons is elevated to the position of Minister of the Crown, notwithstanding the fact that he already possesses the confidence of the people, as shown by his election to the Commons, he is obliged to go back to his constituents for re-election.
That, to me, proves that it was the intention to provide an absolute safeguard; it was intended to ensure that when a man was promoted to the responsible position of Minister of the Crown he should possess the confidence of the electors.
It is no compliment to the hon. members on the other side of the House that three members of the present Cabinet are drawn from the Senate and that the Prime Minister of Canada should, in effect, say to hon. gen- ' tlemen opposite that he does not find any of them worthy of occupying the position of Postmaster General, for instance, or that of Minister of Labour, or whatever it may be. For my part, I believe there are a great many members on the other side of the House who could discharge the duties pertaining to those portfolios fully as well as those duties are now discharged, and it would be more in keeping with the principle of responsible government, because the fact that they occupied seats in this House would be an assurance tnat they possessed the confidence of the people.
In the resolution which I have submitted I provide for a slight qualification, and it is this: that members of the Cabinet shall become members of the House of Commons within a period of three months after their appointment to the Cabinet. I am willing to admit that occasions might arise when
it would be desirable, possibly in an emergency or because of some man's special fitness, to appoint to a Cabinet position a man who was not a member of the House of Commons. In such a case the new minister should submit himself, in accordance with the principle of responsible government, to the electors and be returned to the House of Commons within a period of not longer than three months. Failing to be returned, he should make way for some one else who would fill the requirements in that regard.
I shall not elaborate the matter further. It seems to me the argument requires no proof, that the principles are so sound as to be apparent to all; the truth of what I have said, while it has been poorly expressed, must be evident to almost any member of this House. I base my argument on the simple principle that membership in the Cabinet of Canada should be held only by those who are members of the House of Commons and thus responsible to the people. In these supposedly advanced days of the sovereignty of the people let us show our sincerity by putting our own house in order. Let the Government of Canada conform in every respect with the principle of responsible institutions, for which such heavy sacrifices have been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I have listened with close attention to the observations of my hon. friend (Mr. Euler) with respect to the motion now before the House, and if II have any general criticism to make of his remarks, as I understood them, it is his failure to appreciate the constitution as it is to-day, and the status of the Senate as a body of co-ordinate jurisdiction with this House. My hon. friend's argument proceeded along this line: The Senate is not an elective body, but an appointive body. Therefore, no member of the Government should be a member of the Senate. Now it is debatable-'the hon. member and other hon. gentlemen have their views-whether the Senate of this Parliament should be an elective or an appointive body; but that is not the question before the House. The question before the House is the motion of the hon. member, and that motion must, I submit, be debated having regard to the constitutional position as it exists to-day. It appears to me that to give effect to the resolution of the hon. member would be to derogate from the status of the Senate as established under the British North America Act. I think it might properly be pointed out that the British North America Aot is an act of Union; it is a compact; it represents the agreement which

was made by the different sections^ of this country at the time of Confederation. It is perfectly clear from the debates which preceded Confederation, and from the Act of Union itself, that great importance was attached to the creation of the Senate as a part of Parliament. My hon. friend has put his resolution in this form:
That in the opinion of this House all Ministers of the Crown should be members of the House of 'Commons or become such within a period of three months after their appointment to the Cabinet.
He puts his resolution affirmatively; but, negatively, it might be put in this way- and my hon. friend did put it this way in his remarks:-No member of the Government of Canada shall be a member of the Senate for a longer period than three months. Now in view of the constitutional situation as it exists to-day, namely, that the Senate has under the British North America Act co-ordinate legislative authority with this House, save as to money votes and bills levying taxation upon the people, which must originate with the Commons, it would appear to me that the resolution goes much further than this House or the country would be prepared to go; because it involves a vital change in our constitutional practice of administration and of legislation, and, as I have said, derogates from the status conferred upon the Senate by the British North America Act.
I think I would agree with my hon. friend that the representation of the Government in the Senate should always be limited as compared with that which it should and, I submit, must have in the House of Commons. Ever since Confederation however it has been recognized by all administrations that the Government must be represented in the Senate for the reason that the Senate is a legislative body, that Bills originate with the Senate as well as with the .Commons and that the Senate must be a party to all legislation before it can become law. I do not know that any hard-and-fast principle has been adopted, but it has been generally recognized that there are certain portfolios which must belong to the Commons. For example, I cannot conceive of the Minister of Finance being a member of the Senate and not of the House of Commons, because of course, he is dealing almost wholly with financial and fiscal measures which must originate in the House of Commons. With regard to the British Constitutional system, it is to be observed that a member of government need not necessarily, according to the strict law of the constitution, have 
a seat in the House of Commons or in the Senate. Frequently, and especially upon the formation of new governments, a minister is called into the counsels of the Government by the Prime Minister although he has not a seat in either House. In practice, of course, that situation could not be long maintained, and therefore I may dismiss that feature because, generally speaking, it is necessary that Ministers of the Government should have seats either in the House of Commons or in the Senate for the purpose of dealing with the legislation which is there being discussed, of expounding 'Government measures, and of informing the two Chambers as to government policy. There are certain departments which I think should be represented in the Commons, although I should not like to lay down a hard-and-fast rule. The Department of Finance is clearly one pf them. It has been the practice ever since Confederation, as I have stated, for governments to have representatives in the Senate, and so far as I am aware the leader of the Senate has always been a member of the Government, in order, as is obvious, that he may inform the Senate as to Government policy is regard to legislation before it.
I took the trouble, in connection with this resolution, to look up the practice of the various ministries with regard to Senate representation, and my hon. friend is entirely in error in supposing that this Government is in any singular or anomalous position, much less one open to criticism, by reason of having three members in the Senate. In the Administration of Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Alexander Campbell was Minister of Justice and leader of the Senate; and when Sir John A. Macdonald died, there were, I think, two members of his Administration without portfolio in the Senate. My hon. friend will find that under the succeeding Prime Ministers, Sir John Abbott, Sir John Thompson, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, and Sir Charles Tupper, there was in the case of each Administration a representation of two or three members of the Government in the Senate; and always, I believe, the leader of the Senate, under the Administrations of which I have spoken, was a member of the Government of the day. Further than that, Sir Mackenzie Bowell when Prime Minister was leader of the Senate. Coming down to the Liberal Administration of the late Bight Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier-of whom I have always understood my hon. friend was a devoted follower and admirer-we find that instead of the number of members of the

Government having been diminished in his regime it was if anything enlarged. My hon. friend declares that he is taking advanced Liberal ground. Well, he is criticising rather severely in his remarks some men whom the people thought were fairly advanced Liberals.

-I am quite prepared to allow him to do so; hut I do not know what the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier would have said to him if he had suggested that he, Sir Wilfrid, was not a democrat, and was not in favour of democratic government. I do not know what the late Hon. Sir Oliver Mowat would have said to my hon. friend if he had made the suggestion that he also, although a Liberal, was not in favour of democratic government. And I would point out, with reference to the last-named statesman, who so long carried the banner of Liberalism in the province of Ontario, and indeed in Dominion affairs as well, that when he joined the Liberal Administration in 1896 he became Minister of Justice and at the same time took a seat in the Senate and became its leader. Then there was another noted statesman of whom I used to hear in the old days, and who I thought was a fairly advanced Liberal. I think he would turn in his grave to-night if any hon. gentleman, especially on the other side, suggested that he was not a Liberal and a believer in democratic government. I refer to that old fighting Liberal, the late Sir Richard Cartwright, who became a member of the Senate and its leader, and who, while he occupied that position in the Senate, held one of the most important portfolios in the Government-the portfolio of Trade and Commerce. Would my hon. friend suggest for one moment that any of the departments mentioned here to-night is of more importance to the business and commercial life of the country than the Department of Trade and Commerce? I do not believe the hon. member would put forward that view for an instant. There was another man whose name was known in every Liberal household throughout Canada,-the Hon. Sir Richard Scott. He was a strong Liberal, and I believe that he would have said, and all of his associates would have said, that he was in
favour of democratic government and of the principles of democracy. He was Secretary of State in the Laurier administration and was also a member of the Senate. In addition to those I have mentioned,- Sir Oliver Mowat, Sir Richard Cartwright and Sir Richard Scott-there were, I believe, two other members of the Laurier Administration who had seats in the Senate; one was Hon. Mr. Templeman and the other Mr. Hyman. So that we have an unbroken practice-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend would like to have the Hon. Mr. Hyman and the Hon. Mr. Templeman eliminated, I shall be content with Sir Oliver Mowat, Sir Richard Cartwright and Sir Richard Scott. I was pointing out that all governments since Confederation have had representation in the Senate. So far from defending that system, I put forward the view that with the constitution as it is to-day no other course is practicable. I put that view forward for the reason that the Senate is a body of co-ordinate legislative jurisdiction with this House with the exception that money votes have to originate here as well as bills providing for taxation. Another name that I had overlooked has been called to my attention by an hon. member-that of the Hon. David Mills. No hon. gentleman on the other side of the House would challenge for one moment the Liberalism or fidelity to democratic principles of the Hon. David Mills. Why, he was one of the Apostles of Liberalism. When my hon. friend finds fault with the Union Government for having representation, as we have it to-day, in the Senate, he is by implication visiting very severe

censure upon the liberalism of those who were highest in the counsels of the Liberal party, its leaders and, as I have said, its apostles. I have no doubt that my hon. friend had his early teaching in Liberal principles from those whom he is impliedly censuring to-night by reason of the fact that they concurred in the principle of representation of the Government in the Senate.
I do not know what view my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) will take in regard to this but we shall hear in due course. I am not censuring those leaders of Liberalism. I repeat that under our system as it exists to-day, no other course is open to a government but to have representation in the Senate. Bills originate in this House involving matters of Government policy. Bills also originate in the Senate involving matters of Government policy. For the despatch of business it is very desirable that the Government should be able to initiate Bills in the Senate as well as in the House of Commons if for no other reason than to save time. But even as to Bills originating in the House of Commons and which go to the Senate, they must be adopted there. The policy of the Government must be explained with respect to those Bills because the Senate must concur in them before they can finally receive the assent of the Governor General and become law.
Fancy the situation that would exist with no member of the Government in the Senate to indicate the policy of the Government in regard to particular measures and to guide its deliberations in respect to Bills of any character, financial, fiscal or otherwise, which had been introduced by the Government and carried through this House. It seems perfectly clear to me that there must be representation of the Government in the Senate. I think the leader of the Senate should be a member of the Government. Although I am rather in favour of limiting the number of members of the Government in the Senate, because this is the popular chamber, I see no objection, as the governments of which I have spoken saw no objection, but on the other hand I see an advantage in having representation of the Government of the day in the Senate. Otherwise, I am satisfied that the business of legislation would not proceed with the despatch that is desirable; nor with the co-ordination of work that should exist as between the two Houses.
My hon. friend has spoken about the fact that the Postmaster General and the Minis-

ter of Labour occupy seats in the Senate. In past Administrations the Minister of Justice frequently occupied a seat in the Senate. The Secretary of State in some Administrations occupied a seat in the Senate. The important Department of Trade and Commerce was represented by Sir Richard Cartwright under the Laurier Administration and the important Department of Agriculture has been on more than one occasion represented in the Senate. Where is the difficulty from the standpoint of conveying information to this House as to Estimates or as to the administration of some department which happens to be represented in the Senate. Take the Postmaster General's department, one of his colleagues is here to answer questions which may be asked of the Prime Minister and to deal with his Estimates when they are before the House. Another colleague, the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, is here to represent the Minister of Labour in this Chamber, to answer questions and to declare the position of the Government in regard to any matter which may come within the jurisdiction of that important department. My hon. friend used a very strong term in regard to the Union Government. He does not seem to like the Union Government-it is hard for me to understand that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: There are lots of reasons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: I know that my hon. friend (Mr. Gauvreau) has a very much more kindly feeling towards the Government and he would not express himself in such strong terms. My hon. friend's resolution has stated that the policy of this Government in having the Postmaster General a member of the Senate and the Minister of Labour a member of the Senate is an arrogant defiance of the will of the people. If that is so, it seems to me that he must apply it to the preceding Administration.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
That statement was made
entirely with regard to the retaining of the Postmaster General after the people had expressly declared that he had not their confidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Was it in arrogant defiance of the will of the people for Sir Richard .Cartwright to represent the Liberal government in the Senate? Should he have gone to the country to be elected after having been appointed to the Senate?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: He was not defeated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
confines it to one case, but it seems to me that, if it was arrogant defiance of the will of the people to appoint, under the constitution, a citizen to the Senate, and afterwards appoint him to a membership in the Government, or if he chanced to be a member of the Government to retain him, then I say precisely the same remark must apply in the case of any other citizen, or former minister, who was appointed to the Senate and retained a seat in the Senate and his position in the Government without having been endorsed by the people.
I pointed out that we must take the constitution as it is, and as it is the Senate is an appointed body. This Government is only following the practice of all governments since Confederation in having a portion of its membership represented in the Senate of Canada. I have shown, I think, that for convenience of legislation in the two Houses it is absolutely necessary that the Government should be represented there, and in view of all the considerations put forward, it would appear to me that this House would be very slow indeed to adopt a resolution of such far-reaching effect, so far-reaching as to seriously affect the legislative machinery of this country, set up at the time of Confederation, and consisting as it does, not only of the House of Commons, but of the Senate. So long as the Senate is a part of our constitution, until the constitution is changed it appears to me that this Government, or succeeding Governments, will be found to have a representation in the Senate if they are to have proper regard to the efficient despatch of the legislation which comes before Parliament.
It is not necessary that I should refer to the situation which exists in Great Britain. My honourable friend would hardly contend that Great Britain is not a democracy. Great Britain has been fighting the battle of democracy in this war, and has been pretty successful in fighting it. It has been the democratic spirit which has animated Britain which has enabled her to win the war, but what is the practice there? We find that in democratic Britain Lord Kitchener was Minister of War, and occupied a seat in the Lords. Will my honourable friend contend that Lord Kitchener was debarred from occupying the position of Minister of War at the outbreak of hostilities because he occupied a seat in the House of Lords? And what shall we say with regard to Lord Milner and Lord Curzon?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Is the Acting Prime Minister giving those as examples of British democracy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I have no hesitation in giving the Right Honourable Lloyd George as a shining example of British democracy. My honourable friend would not dissent from that surely? And my honourable friend knows how the Right Honourable Lloyd George has constituted his government to-day. So that I think we can put on one side the talk about the violation of democratic principle in this Government having three representatives in the Senate.
Now my honourable friend has put forward his resolution and delivered a very interesting speech in support of it. I have given the reasons which, in my view, should influence the House in rejecting it. I think that while the constitution remains as it is we should not lay down the principle in this House that no Government should have one or more of its members in the Senate, which is a component part of Parliament, and, in my view therefore the resolution should be negatived.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton South and Victoria):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not find
it necessary in answering the argument of the honourable leader of the Government, to make any pronouncement as to any views that I may entertain myself in regard to whether or not members of the Senate should be members of this, or any Government. The honourable member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has put his case very clearly and very strongly, and I think that in a democratic country like Canada, and in a democratic House such as this, it is well that questions of this kind should be brought forward and discussed in the open so that people in the country may know what our views are. In my humble judgment, Mr. Speaker, the leader of the Government did not answer the argument of the mover of the resolution at all. The honourable member for North Waterloo admitted that it has been the practice since Confederation for members of the Senate to be members of the various governments. Notwithstanding this admission the leader of the Government, having no other course, built up this man of straw, and when he had that effigy well built and of very good proportions, started in to demolish it. He made a fairly good job of demolishing his straw man. because there was nobody to interfere-the effigy was unprotected from his very vigor-



ous attack. There is no question about any man's ability to put up that kind of man and knock him down. But that is not the question at all. The question is whether or not in this democratic country, in this great Canada of ours, at this parti-
9	p.m. cular juncture when we say that old things have passed away, when this democratic Union Government which we now have tells us that everything has become new-there are no Grits, there are not even any Tories according to its dictum. The old landmarks, they tell us, are forever swept away, or put to one side. Such being the doctrine, and gospel of the Union Government, if everything else of old habits must disappear, and forever, this undemocratic idea of members of an irresponsible body being members of a responsible government, should also disappear? That is the spirit, object, and principle of the resolution of the' hon. member for North Waterloo. But the leader of the Government says there must be Government representation in the Senate. I agree that it is and has been the custom to have a member of the Government in the Senate as a sort of intermediary between that House and the Government.
It does not follow that the man who is that intermediary should have any particular responsibility to the people of this country or should be an administrator at all. Up to a short time ago Sir James Lougheed, although the recognized leader of the Government in the Senate, had no portfolio, and with that condition of affairs no person had any fault to find. But the moment that a man who is a senator and not responsible to the people, a man who cannot be called upon to go before the electorate and give an account of his stewardship, becomes the spender of the people's money as the Senate may tell him to expend it, he should be responsible to the people. It is absolutely impossible, Mr. Speaker, to think of responsible Government if that is not done, because the true essence and meaning of responsible Government is that the Government collectively and individually is responsible to the people and must submit its actions to their final judgment. If that Administration is to a large extent governed by a body that is not obliged to go to the electorate for a verdict in favour of or against its Administration, it is no longer responsible. It is along those lines that my hon. friend moving this resolution is asking the opinion of this House.

Now, let me say to the hon. leader of the Government that only a few days ago-last Friday, was it not?.-he took a spasmodic fit in favour of wide-open democracy in the shape of the Daylight Saving Bill; but I think, as was hinted on this side of the House, that was something that he was quite willing to get clear of, he was willing to be generous in disposing of that he hated to have anything to do with, and he let us have our full fling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: A final fling.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
He said in effect,
" They think they are having something they are really not getting, and I am delighted to be clear of it and to let them get into all the hot -water they please over it." But now when it comes down to a question that is more democratic, that goes to the very heart of democracy-and we have some very good democrats in this House-[DOT] he cracks the whip at his followers and says, "This must not be accepted," and whether our friends, the supporters of the Government, think this is a democratic idea or not, the ground is cut from under their feet and they must not think at all for themselves, but simply as the Government thinks.
The leader of the Government put forward a few arguments as to why we should have representation in the Senate. If we turn to the Government of the United States, Mr. Speaker, we find that it is governing a hundred million people and has not a representative in either the Senate or the House of Representatives. Still it gets along splendidly, and if the United States Government gets along with the governing of a hundred million people without a representative in Congress, surely this Canada of ours with only eight million people, having full representation of the Government through elected members of this House, can get along without a representative in the Senate.
iMy hon. friend is a good lawyer, and I presume above everything else he is a good constitutional lawyer. I am sure he is not trying to tell us that the Senate is in all respects the same as this House as far as the representation of the people is concerned. He tells us that it is important that the Senate should know what the Government policy is. They have nothing to do, Sir, with Government policy; they are supposed to be paid by the people as an independent body, as a check upon the legislation of this House, absolutely free from party bias one way or the other. That is their function, and that is their position.

It is not necessary therefore, if they are properly discharging that function, to tell them how the wind blows as far as Government policy is concerned; although I do not object to somebody being in the Government without portfolio who can tell the Senate what the policy of the Government is, but they are not so very busy but they might read Hansard and see what is going on in this House. Perhaps it is necessary to chew the food for them and put it in their mouths, but I do not think that is the type of men they are. I think they are willing to read the Bills we send down for their consideration without somebody going over them and telling them what is in them. I do not think it is at all necessary that, on the grounds set forth by the hon. gentleman we should have members of the Senate in the Government.
Now about the question of Labour. The hon. minister knows that that is a department of comparatively recent origin. It has been created for the purpose of giving labour a special voice in this House through a minister, and if there is any department of our Government that requires to be in immediate touch with the legislative body, that department is the Department of Labour, because every hour something arises in this House, some questions to be asked by the men who are here fresh from the people and who are in touch with labour feelings and labour wants. There should be a man sitting in this House, and I submit to tbe Acting Prime Minister that it was always the intention from the inception of this Department of Labour that the minister presiding over it would be in this House. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Government that they have no business to take the Minister of Labour, I care not how excellent a man he may be, and place him in the seclusion of the Senate where we who represent labour have never an opportunity of presenting our views to him. He should be sitting in this House and hearing what we say.
I have no advice to give my hon. friend who moved this resolution. I do not wish to establish a precedent that my hon. friend who leads the Government might think would be detrimental J,o the established principles that we have been following in this country, but I think the purpose of the resolution would be served just as well if it were not pressed to a vote.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) has so well answered the arguments of the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) that very little is
m
left for me to say. The Acting Prime Minister, being a lawyer, apparently has more respect for precedent than I have. I admitted that the practice we have discussed to-night has been followed in the past, but I am not prepared to admit that because of that it was a correct practice to follow. After all, the Acting Prime Minister was quoting persons in the way of precedents, whereas I was trying to impress principles. He has not answered the argument that ministers in charge of important portfolios [DOT] involving the expenditure of large sums of money should be responsible to the people through the Parliament of Canada. And the vital principle involved in this case of the Postmaster General he has avoided with great skill.
The Acting Prime Minister paid considerable attention to what may be called the constitutional phase of the question. He said that it was in accordance with the constitution that we should have members of the Cabinet in the Senate. I do not think it is mandatory or obligatory that members of the Senate should be in the Cabinet; the matter is entirely subject to the discretion of the Prime Minister or of the Cabinet itself. I am inclined to think, from the tenor of his remarks, that the Acting Prime Minister is, after all, pretty much in sympathy with what I have stated. In fact, he gave expression to the opinion that he would not like to see-he did not use the word "abuse," but I will do so

the abuse carried much further. In view of that assertion, and having regard to the probability that as a result of this we may expect an abatement of an unsound practice, and because of the fact that the Acting Prime Minister has cracked the party whip, I shall not press the motion to a division.
