QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO INCLUDE BOYS ENLISTED UNDER AGE.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, hoys who enlisted under age and who under the regulations are not at present Included in the present vocational system, shall be given vocational training in such lines as may be considered to their best interest and so as to enable them to complete their educational course interfered with by enlistment. [DOT]
He said: Mr. Speaker, in bringing this resolution before the House I feel that the principle which it embodies will receive a very large measure of sympathy and support from the members of the House, and,

I am quite sure, from the Government. I have purposely limited the resolution so that it applies only to boys enlisted under age. My reason for doing so was this. Many difficulties are involved in the question of vocational training in its wide, broad sense, and I recognize the perplexities with which the Government was faced in deciding just how far to go. I did feel that there could be no opposition to dealing with the class referred to in this resolution, and I made this limitation specifically to enable the Government to get the views of the House with regard to the matter. I feel sure that they will remedy this very serious defect in the system of vocational training. The great dominion of Australia has adopted this system. I state that simply as a suggestion, not particularly as an argument.
The lads who enlisted at the age of fifteen, sixteen, seventeen and eighteen, will be citizens of Canada for a long time. They are young men, starting at the very-threshold of life, and for the full term of their manhood will be citizens of the country. Parliament, therefore, would assume a very serious responsibility if it interfered in any way with the prospects in life of a young man just at the beginning of his career. That is a very strong point that I wish to emphasize at the outset.
The State owes the boyhood of Canada a fair chance. The citizen owes allegiance, support and loyalty to the State; but the State has its duty to the citizen. These lads demonstrated their loyalty to the State by volunteering their services,-many of them gave up their lives at the front,- and to young fellows of that type the State owes everything they can do for them. II an error was made in allowing these young men to enlist and go overseas, the error was on the part of the -State, not on the part of the boy. The boy simply showed a splendid spirit, the spirit which actuated the manhood of Canada generally; they went overseas typifying the sacrifice, and the grit, and the pluck, of the people of Canada. I wish to give one or two illustrations to bear out my arguments. A young lad enlisted at sixteen years of age and went overseas with the 65th Battalion. He received his certificate for entering High iSchool before he enlisted. He was wounded at Regina Trench. Certain great battles or events of the war stand out from others; one of these is Regina Trench. Any boy who went through that fight and who suffered wounds there is certainly entitled to consideration. This lad has since recovered and returned to Canada after several years' service. He
rMr. Stevens.]
finds himself faced with a regulation which provides that as he is not incapacitated to carry on his previous work he is not entitled to vocational training. What was his previous work? He was a schoolboy. Mark you, this boy goes overseas, performs all the work of a man, heroically faces the enemy, suffers wounds, comes back a full-grown man-because no person could question his manhood after that-and he is asked to go back to school again where he left off, two, three, or four years before, as the case may . be. The perpetuation of such a regulation is too absurd to be seriously, considered 'by. the House.
Another is the case of two brothers who went overseas. The younger enlisted at the age of fifteen. He was a big, husky boy, but the authorities knew he was under age and they kept him in Canada for six or seven months. The boy however was keen to get across and he got an opportunity to go over with one of the battalions. He was engaged in a number of battles and was wounded twice. His elder brother was also wounded, returned, and got vocational training, but this younger boy comes back to Canada and gets no vocational training at all, because when asked his vocation on enlisting he said he was a photographer. As a matter of fact he was a messenger to a photographer in Montreal. They gave him a physical examination when he returned, felt him all over and finding him physically sound, told him:	" You can
carry on as a photographer which was what you were engaged at before enlisting." That is another illustration, and I could give very many more.
I have here a document drawn up by students of Queen's University giving another viewpoint. Briefly, it is this: Some 110, or something like sixty per cent, of the second-year medical students at Queen's -I think the figures are limited to Queen's -went overseas and gave their trained services as orderlies in hospitals; they were not qualified to go as medical men, but gave their two years' training in the university for the benefit of the hospitals, as orderlies. They come back after a couple of years' service without any funds, for they -could save Very little out of an ' orderly's pay, and now they need -assistance to complete their third year. Most of them are young fellows; some of them, though perhaps not all, under age. That is but another illustration of the imperative necessity of this House and Government recognizing the need of helping the boys to carry on their educational courses an l

fitting them for their vocation in life, whatever that may he.
I wish to proceed to another argument, and what I shall say is not in the way of criticism, because all this work is new to the Government and to the country, but simply in the way of suggestion to the Government. My opinion is that our present method of vocational training is too diversified; it is not under one head. It may be answered that, technically speaking, there is a head in Ottawa, but I am speaking not of the ministerial, but of the technical or professional head. As a matter oi fact the training is not under one head so far as administration is concerned. In that respect each unit-and there are something like a dozen different units in Canada- carries on almost independently. Let me give an illustration of one unit with which I have some acquaintance-"J" unit, which is the unit of the province of British Columbia. On the staff of "J" unit are 57 returned men, 9 civilians, and 25 female assistants, mostly stenographers. That makes a staff of 91, which is divided as follows: 38 instructors, 8 ward aids,-that is women who assist in the wards with the cases confined to bed-and 45 administrators. There we have only 46 instructors out of	a	staff	of 91,
and I do submit that the proportion may fairly be considered as almost top heavy. The reason I draw attention to this matter is that I believe the work could be done far better if it were under a head with some special qualifications-a man, for instance, who had been a sub-head of one of our leading educational institutions or universities. A man trained in technical educational work should have supreme control of vocational training in Canada, and each unit should carry on under this central head.
Another point I wish to make in that connection is this: Instead of giving training in electrical engineering, we will say, in each of these different units, it might be very much more to the advantage of the student, and would certainly be to the advantage of the country from a financial standpoint, if the training in these various vocations could be centralized to a greater degree than at present. I will illustrate what I mean by again referring to "J" unit. In "J" unit there are certain centres where vocational training is given. At Fairmont hospital in Vancouver, I find, there are six teachers and five pupils. It is difficult to understand just what the six teachers are doing witli only
five pupils,-perhaps one of the pupils is particularly unruly. At another place, I find two teachers and twenty-four pupils; at another, three teachers and seventy-four pupils; at another, fourteen teachers and one hundred and fifty-nine pupils. The latter three cases are quite reasonable. At Esquimalt there are four teachers and fifteen pupils. The reason I draw the attention of the Government to this is because I believe the cost of administration, which is always advanced as an argument against expenditure on vocational training, could be very materially reduced and the efficiency of the training very much increased; and if a reorganization were effected, not one iota would be added to the cost of extending this education to the young men with whom particularly my resolution deals. Some time ago I asked some questions which have not yet been answered, and which were asked to stand as an order for a return, which has not yet been received, so I am not in a position to give exact data upon this point, but I am informed that there nave been between six and seven hundred applications for vocational training from young boys who enlisted under age which have been turned down; I do not know how many more there are. Let us compare this number who would be affected by my resolution with the number of applications received,-and I do this to show that it is not such a very important matter from the standpoint of finances as we might be led to believe. I am told that Ithe total applications for vocational training are somewhere around 12,000-from 11,900 to 12,000. That is quite a large number and will give the House an idea of the magnitude of the task which the Government have in hand. Now the point I make is this: That the administration cost for additional pupils would be comparatively slight compared with the administration cost of the training now given, and particularly so if a better organization of the system of training were effected.
I wish at this point to ask a question which I think is of vital importance. If we refuse these boys this technical or vocational training, what is to become of them?
They left the country as boys out of High school or college, or from the shop; they were merely lads playing around their homes. They leave, and in a couple of years are transformed into men-a transformation that, had they remained in civil life, it would have taken probably ten or lifteen years to effect. Tt is unreasonable to expect that these lads in any large num-

ber will go quietly back to school to resume their education at the point at which they left off. If they will not do that-as I am sure they will not-what is their future to be? There is only one thing open to them, that is, the common labour market; I say emphatically- that it would be wrong to take keen-spirited lads like these-because they were the keenest-spirited of all who enlisted-and, after they have been to the front and have rendered such admirable service, many of them returning seriously wounded, simply turn them loose and say, " Now you can go to the pick and shovel." This Parliament and this country owe to every one of them at the very least a technical education. We owe them the chance of making good in this life, and it is our bounden duty to see that they get that chance. I accordingly urge this resolution, and would bespeak for it the most serious and careful attention of the Government.	,
At this point I would offer another suggestion, and that is in reference to the establishment of technical schools in Canada. I believe, Sir, that this is an excellent opportunity for the Government to take advantage of the suggestions put forward in a very long report on technical education made some years ago under the authority, I think of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier's Government. I remember having seen the report, although I had not the time to give it any careful perusal. It strongly advocated the establishment of technical schools in Canada, and if ever there was a necessity for such institutions it surely exists to-day, not only for these lads but also for other men who have been wholly or partially incapacitated. Technical schools are urgently needed, and this would be an eminently opportune time to establish them and make them a permanent institution. I do not think that there is an hon. member in the House, or an intelligent citizen in the country who will question the advisability of establishing such schools. Taking that for granted, when could a better opportunity present itself for the undertaking than at this moment? For these reasons I would impress upon the Government, and particularly upon the minister in charge of this department, the importance of technical schools for the instruction of the youths who enlisted under age as well as other men seeking technical education or vocational training. I do not desire to labour the question, but the problem facing us is one which not only merits our attention, but imposes a

serious duty upon us, and I trust the Government will not pass it off with the comment that the matter is a complicated one which may open the door to serious and expensive demands from all quarters, but will realize, in its fullest significance, the fact that there are some six or seven hundred lads who enlisted underage and did their bit and who have now come back with the simple request that they be given a decent technical education to fit them for their future life work. The very least that a grateful government and people can do is to give these lads the opportunity they deserve and badly need, and for these reasons I move the resolution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this question first came up Canada did what I think every other country at war did. It regarded disability as the line of division between men who should be re-trained and men who should not. This was the only line that could be taken by which we could avoid what might be considered as class legislation. It may probably be argued that we have strayed from that in connection with our Soldiers' Settlement Act when we re-train men to enter into agriculture. But as against this argument it must be remembered that our object was to encourage the returned Soldiers to take up agriculture, and the object of the re-training was to ascertain whether or not the applicants were fit and proper persons to whom certain loans should be given to enable them to go into farming. Outside of that I think we can say that we have so far avoided anything that might be called class legislation. I admire my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in the sympathetic attitude he takes towards the men who enlisted under age, because I am firmly convinced they were impelled by a splendid spirit of patriotism, a spirit perhaps not shown by others of ma-turer years; I believe, as he does, that the Government should have some regard for these young men who have devoted two, three or four of the most precious years of their lives to the service of their country -years in which their characters were forming, and in which they and their parents hoped they would be able to qualify in some profession or occupation by which to earn their livelihood.
My hon. friend suggests that he does not want to hear any reasons why this project should not be undertaken, but I must tell him that when it was first proposed it opened the door to other propositions as

well. The proposal was made to us by the universities, to which it was represented by the returned men that those who wished to have an education should he given it. We had the further demand that other people who were not students should be compensated for losses in business, or should be given loans to set them up in business, and the subject assumed such large proportions that the Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment decided to go no further with it. This, however, was owing to no lack of sympathy with the proposal my hon. friend has just advanced. The entire subject of university training has engaged the attention of the Repatriation Committee of the Government, a member of which committee will no doubt speak after I have concluded. .The university students whose courses were interrupted, and who, perhaps, are in as bad a position as young men who enlisted under age, must also be considered, and that is a matter that will have to come before the Government. I can well understand the arguments of my hon.- friend with respect to all these classes of men. He has anticipated the contention that might be made as regards increased cost, by giving us the cost of organization and of maintenance, and he has suggested that there should be more centralization. Had I expected these arguments I might, be in a better position to meet them. However, I wish to say that the young men in whom my hon. friend has shown such sympathetic interest have the same interest and sympathy from myself.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO INCLUDE BOYS ENLISTED UNDER AGE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that so small a House is present to consider the question which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has brought to the fore. I also regret that I have made no preparation to address the House on this subject, but it is one that I have been interested in and I would like therefore to have a word upon it. If the wealth of the country is its manhood, as we all believe, this question is one that very greatly concerns the future of our Canadian soldiers, and more especially is it necessary that we should deal with the very young men of the class which the hon. member for Vancouver has dealt with. The very young man has not fixed his course in life; he has not as yet set before him what his life aim shall be, as the university student or the man who has chosen a professional course has. There will be a very serious void in this young man's life unless an unusual effort is made to engage his interest in its future development. I believe that Parliament is
interested in getting this young man started upon a course of vocational training, the machinery for which has been largely provided. It is not a matter of extending it to the young men who can be brought into the schools and technical colleges which the Government will operate apart in any event from the question of training injured soldiers. I therefore would give my support to the proposition and earnestly commend it to the House.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not expect to take part in this debate, but I think something should be said in support of the proposition brought forward by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. In my humble opinion, the State owes a very special debt to those boys of fifteen or sixteen who went to the front, because they never should have been allowed to go. If the State allowed them to go to the front, then the State is under an obligation to see that they are equipped to lead useful lives when they come back. I was somewhat astonished to hear the remarks made by the hon. Acting Parliamentary Secretary of the Department oi Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment (Mr. Hugh Clark). What I gathered from his remarks was that a claim was made to this Government on behalf of those boys that they should be entitled to vocational training, and that apparently this was a just claim; that again a demand was made for special training by people who had lost money, and that that was not such a just claim as the other; that these matters constituted a proposition of such tremendous importance and difficulty to the Government that the only thing they could offer to the boys at the present time was warm and sincere sympathy. I think that the young men who are in a position that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has brought before the House are entitled to something more.

speechtext:
No doubt they are engaging the attention of the Government, but that the war was going to come to an end was an idea that we had been cherishing for years. Incidents of this class ought to have been considered months ago rather than, as the Government tell us, after the boys come home and are discharged from

the army. It is during the first few months after they are discharged that they must be interested in some line or they will drift into those blind alleys of employment that the member for Vancouver Centre indicated. I endorse most heartily what has been said by hon. members on the other side of the House, and urge that this matter is of paramount and immediate importance. It seems to me that the Government has only to amend its regulations so as to say that all the school hoys who left Canada and who served in the army should, on their return, have the right to vocational training even if they do not come within the four corners of the present regulations. speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Council):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO INCLUDE BOYS ENLISTED UNDER AGE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question
brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) is one of very great importance and I am sure all the members of the House are deeply interested in it. 1 believe the number under the age of eighteen years who enlisted, is substantially larger than my hon. friend mentions. I have not the final figures but the estimate which I have received, and which is based on the information the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment has secured is between 5,000 and 7,000. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) suggested that the enlistment of these boys should not have been permitted. I imagine that very few were knowingly permitted. I imagine that the boys gave their ages as 18 years or more in order to get overseas. I believe there were many instances of that kind. T remember on one occasion being at a camp in Prance where I saw a boy who was obviously under 18 years of age. I also saw a man who was obviously over military age. I said to the man who was over military age: How did this boy get over here? He turned to the boy and said: How do you come to be here? The boy replied: I got here in the same way as you did-by lying about my age. Many of the boys in their anxiety to get over, gave an age above what it actually was.
I am only saying that in answer to what my hon. friend said that the Government should not have permitted them to enlist. But that they constituted an exceedingly fine body of young men no one will ques-
(Mr. McMnstor. |
tion. I remember many of them were brought back from France when it was found that they were under age. Last summer we saw at Bramshott a full battalion of young boys under the command of Colonel McKay of Winnipeg.
Some of those boys had one or two wound stripes on their arm, and I must say I never saw a finer battalion- than that battalion composed of boys all under eighteen years of age. The majority of them had served at the front. Others had gone as far as England and were weeded out of other battalions and incorporated in this boys' battalion under the comnland of an able and sympathetic commanding officer, who was giving them training in England.
Now, as my hon. friend from North Bruce (Mr. Clark) has pointed out, the basis upon which the work of the vocational branch of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is carried on is to provide an education for disabled soldiers, a disability of the soldier which prevents him from resuming his former occupation, and the training courses are established and carried on to fit him for a new pursuit. May I turn to the section of the Order in Council which defines the conditions upon which a man becomes entitled to vocational training under the regulations as they now exist:
Any former member of the forces suffering from a disability which in the opinion of a naval or military medical board, or of a medical officer of the department, is due to or was aggravated by service, and which in the opinion of the Directors of Vocational Training of the Department prevents such former member of the forces from returning to his previous trade or principal occupation, shall be entitled to retraining for a new occupation in accordance with the regulations of the department, and to such allowances as are provided herein for former members of the forces undergoing re-training.
A great many men come within that class, and vocational training is now being carried on throughout the country at the various centres as established by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. That training may be described under three heads.
There is the training which is being given in certain universities and schools to those who desire to enter upon a course, or a vocation, which justifies the sending of them to these schools. In other cases, where special training is required, it has beeen found necessary to establish classes conducted entirely by the department. The third method is the utilization in industries of the apprentice system, where these men are given training in shops or factories in

the particular occupation which they desire to pursue, and their income is supplemented as provided in the Order in Council.
From all who have come within the classes I have referred to, special provision is made by way of pay and allowances. The allowance payable by the department to a former member of the forces who is without dependents will be $60 per month. He receives $60 a month during the whole period he is undergoing this training, as well as free instruction in the school. The allowances payable while undergoing training by the department, for a former member of the forces, who has a wife, or a wife and child, or a wife and children, is as follows:
For such former member of the
Forces	 $85.00 amonth
For one child	 10.00 a month
For two children	 18.00 a month
For three children	 25.00 a month
For more than three children ..	25.00 a month
Plus $6 a month for each child in excess of
three.
The House wilKthiis see and realize the amount that is being contributed by the Government in the case of each of these disabled men, or for a disabled man who has a wife and children. Then, corresponding allowances are made where he is a widower with dependent children. Corresponding allowances are also made where the man, though not married, has others dependent upon him, as in the case with the soldier serving at the front. In other words his position is kept as nearly as possible as it was while he was serving in the army, and he draws pay and allowances during the period he is undergoing training.
It is quite Liue, as has been pointed cut, that this provision does not apply to those who are not disabled, and this raises a very important question. It applies with particular force to those under eighteen years of age. But, as my hon. friend from North Bruce (Mr. Hugh Clark) has mentioned, it has been pressed upon the Government that the relief should not be limited to those under eighteen years, but that provision should be made for all whose education has been interrupted. It is only necessary to point out that the average cost per man of vocational training is about $1,000, to indicate the amount of the charge which would be placed upon the country if many thousands more were brought within the provisions of the existing regulations.

speechtext:
Quite so, that would reduce the administration charge undoubtedly. The number undoubtedly will steadily and rapidly increase as the troops come back, and as the disabled men return from the hospitals in England. Therefore it is-anticipated that there will be a large increase in the number that even under the existing regulations will require treatment in the vocational institutions provided:.. While that is all true, everything that has been said about these boys is also perfectly true. Undoubtedly it is a mat-
10	p.m. ter of serious moment to Canada, and to all the nations at war, that so large a percentage of young men, just at the age when character is being formed, and when they must get their education, if they are to get it under the most advantageous conditions, were called upon to serve their country at the front and have been deprived of these educational opportunities. Unless these young men do receive an education now we will undoubtedly suffer in the future in the educational leadership of our country. I am sure all will recognize that at no period of our history was it more important that we should have our citizens, and particularly those who will be the leaders of our people, thoroughly trained and given the best education that is available in order that they may render to the State the ser-' vice which that education should qualify them to render. As my hon. friend (Mr. Hugh Clark) has said, this whole problem is receiving the earnest consideration of the Government. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment is looking into the number who will be affected by a provision for those under eighteen years. We are also looking into the question of the boys whose university course has been interrupted, to see what financial obligation would be involved if anything is attempted in that direction. This question has been considered by the Repatriation Committee of the Cabinet, and a report has been prepared upon the matter, which will come before the Government for consideration probably within a few days. In view of that fact I must ask my hon. friend, who has very properly brought this matter to the attention of the House, if, having done so, he could see his way clear to withdraw the motion. It is a matter involving

governmental policy which is receiving the earnest attention of the Government at the present time, and upon which an announcement may be expected in the near future.
One other matter I might mention. My honourable friend referred to technical education and the opportunity this would offer the Government for dealing with the suggestions contained in the report on technical education which was made some few years ago by the Commission appointed by the Government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Might I draw my honourable friend's attention to the fact that in the Speech from the Throne there is an announcement that a Bill will be brought down this session providing for vocational training. A Bill will be introduced into the House this session dealing with the question and providing substantial assistance for the work of technical education in the different provinces of the Dominion. There can be no doubt of the importance of technical education, of the great practical benefits which would result to the industrial life of the country if we had a larger trained body, such as we might secure by the enlargement of existing institutions or the establishment of others where technical education might be given.
Mr. WILLIAM F. NICKLE (Kingston): Mr. Speaker, before this resolution is withdrawn by its mover I would like to say a word or two on behalf of the principle enunciated during the debate. As the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) has said, to avoid legislation being thought to be class legislation, those responsible for the promulgation of the regulations affecting vocational training established the principle that vocational training should only be given to those who through disability had been impaired in their trade or occupation as practised before the war. That admits that the soldier prior to enlistment-not the schoolboy, but the soldier who had a trade or occupation-was in a position then to earn his living, and that if his disability was. of such a character that on his return he could not earn his living, then the State recognized its responsibility to give him such a training as would enable him to earn a living in another sphere of activity. But when you come to apply that principle to the position of the schoolboy, you find yourself confronted with this difficulty. The schoolboy at the time of his enlistment-and I am speaking now particularly of the boy in our high schools .and our secondary schools-was not in a position

to earn a living; he was building the foundation on which he hoped later on to earn a living. He went over as a boy of sixteen or seventeen, the companion of girls at school with short skirts and flowing curls and of boys in knickerbockers-children so to speak living at home, kept in the parental establishment at the minimum of cost. He spent two, three or four years at the front. He returned, not a boy of seventeen, but a man of twenty-one, and not only a man of twenty-one in years, but a man of probably twenty-five in experience, in aspirations and in instincts. He cannot return to the secondary school which he left three or four years ago, he must go into the university, where his class fees are greater, and his maintenance higher, and where the general average of living costs are much more than when he was ,a schoolboy.
What is going to become of the young man? He cannot go back to school, because there	is no	place	there	for	him.If means are not provided for him	and-il	speak of	him	who
has not been born with a silver spoon in his mouth-if he has not the means to eon-tiue his education he must give it up. If he had not a trade or occupation prior to going to the war, what is he to do? Because he was willing to sacrifice his future when seventeeen years of age is he to go back to the very roughest of trades, to become a manual labourer? I do not believe that that is the desire or the intention of the Government, and I am impressed to-night by what the President of the Privy 'Council said, that this Government appreciates the necessities of the situation and is endeavouring to find a solution for them. And the President of the Privy 'Council is quite correct when he says that the problem does not stop with the boy who went to the front when he was seventeeen years of age. I am confronted in my own riding, more particularly in the university with which I happen to have the honour to be connected, with the troubles of the medical students and students of the 'School of 'Science. The universities did magnificently in the war. I have not the figures as fully as I would have had them had I any expectation of this debate, but I know the Royal Military College lost in the neighbourhood of 150 of its graduates and undergraduates; that Toronto University lost somewhere in the neighbourhood of 550; that McGill-I regret I have not the figures-

speechtext: A very large contribution.

speechtext:
-but I know McGill gave a magnificent contribution to the war, and Queen's University sacrificed 150 of its graduates and under-graduates. But not only did we sacrifice many men through death, many of our best-and they were the leaders in university life- were impelled by the call of duty when war broke out to go to the front in the most, I was going to say menial, capacity. Medical students of three and four years' standing went as hospital orderlies earning only enough to keep them at the front. Then when they return t>
Canada after giving two or three years from the creative period of their life they find that the six months' course has been extended to eight months, and when they look about to seek employment to put them through they find in these disturbed times that there is no employment to be had, and they are obliged either to seek financial assistance or abandon their course. Last Saturday when in Kingston I was waited upon by a delegation of medical students who explained to me, speaking for their class, that unless they were granted assistance by way of donation, or unless some other financial arrangements were made, it was impossible for many of them to see how their academic course could be completed.
The universities are impressed with the necessity of making up to these young men the years they have lost in the war, and some of them this year are running summer sessions so that a man who is anxious because of the lack of the wherewithal for the more extended course may in two years take the four years' course, that is, in one-half the ordinary academic course he can fit himself for his chosen profession.
I sincerely trust that the Government will give this matter most careful and immediate consideration, because I am impressed with this fact, that if there is one class more than another that has paid a terriffic penalty in this war it is that class which is composed of the leading spirits in our university and educational life, and in the years to come it is absolutely essential that as promptly as possible these men who went down to death be replaced by other men of the same high spirit, vigour of thought and intellectual quality, if Canada is not to feel more severely than she should the sacrifices she has been called upon to make in this war.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO INCLUDE BOYS ENLISTED UNDER AGE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not anything particular to add to what has been so well said by the mover of the resolution and by the other hon. gentlemen -who have spoken, but silence on my part, on account of the position which I hold, might be construed as indicating that I have no special interest in this resolution, when the contrary is the fact. I agree entirely with what has been said by the mover of the resolution as to the very great importance of allowing those young men to get within the scope of the vocational training which is now being given, Nothing should be allowed to stand in the way. I suggest to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), who seems to speak with authority for the Government on this question, that no time be lost in enabling these young men to get the advantages which others are receiving from this branch of education. The country generally has reason to find fault with the Government for being slow in connection with these matters.
The member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) mentioned technical education. That is a matter that has been receiving the attention of this House for many years. Ever since 1910, when a commission was appointed by the Government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier to inquire into the matter, it has received the attention of the country in concrete form. The Government of Sir Robert Borden, early in its lifetime, found in its archives the report of this Commission. I have distinct recollection of this matter coming up in the House every year and of promises repeatedly made that some action would be taken. But eight years have gone by and nothing has been done either by this Government or by the Government preceding it-which was, to my mind, just the same Government under a somewhat different name. And to-night when a supporter of the Government asks wha1 is to be done about technical education, he is told that somewhere, sometime, something may come forth into actuality. Technical education is at all times important; to-day it is more important than ever. If the Government wish to give the industries of this country a good start and a good standing, let them stop high protection and devote their attention to technical education. The industries will then be put upon a good footing, efficiency will be brought about in our producing centres, and oui manufacturing industries will have such r superior standing in the world that protection will no longer be required. I make this argument not in a broad sense of talking politics or tariffs, but simply to illustrate the great necessity of putting

the young men and young women who are to be the producers of our country on an equal footing with those of any other part of the world by giving them technical training.
In the province from which I come we have an excellent technical college; I am proud to say that Nova Scotia was the first province, with its small means, to build up a first class institution of that kind. That technical college is affiliated with the universities in our own province; students holding two-years' certificates from any recognized college in Canada may finish the other two years in our technical college and get their degree. I do not know how many of the other provinces have similar institutions, but I am sure that institutions of that kind can be made sufficiently strong and sufficiently important to be self-sustaining and to be of great benefit not only to the provinces in which they are established, but to the whole country as well. After we get well on our feet in establishing these institutions throughout the provinces, we could have a great central institution for the whole of Canada. But, to begin with, we should have institutions in the various provinces, supported by such sums of money out of the Treasury of the country as will enable them to be put upon a first class and efficient footing and carry on such technical education as is recommended by the Robertson Commission Report now in the hands of the Government.
I fully agree with the arguments put forth by the mover of this resolution, and I hope that what he has in mind will be carried out at once by those who have charge of vocational training; and, further, that the matter of technical education and the carrying out of the terms of the report to which I have referred will be taken up by the Government as soon as possible. I hope that the Government will move; I hope they will start up and do some work. We on this side of the House are ready to meet them and help them along. From day to day, when items of Government work on the Order Paper are reached, the response is given: "Stand"-[DOT] "Stand"-"Stand"- nobody ready to do anything. When we come to have a long dreary session in the hot summer, we shall be blamed on this side for blocking the business of the House, 'whereas we are doing nothing of the kind. We invite the Government to get along with their work, and we will help them; we will help them particularly with this technical education and in the carrying out of the ideas sug-

gested by the resolution of the member for Vancouver Centre.

speechtext: The Acting Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment (Mr. Hugh Clark), said that the basis upon which vocational training was granted to returned soldiers was that of disability. I appreciate, as I stated a moment ago, the perplexities with which those administering this department have been faced; but I think they have had sufficient experience now to have the matter well in hand. I should like to emphasize the fact that I have limited the application of the resolution to boys who enlisted under age. This, I think, is a fair answer to the suggestion that it opens the door to many other claims. The President of the Privy Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) stated that my figures were very much out when I gave 700 as the number of applicants of boys under age for vocational training. He gives the alarming figure of 5,000.

speechtext: My hon. friend will pardon me; I gave 5,000 not as the number of applicants, but as the number under age who enlisted.

speechtext:
I say that this figure is an alarming one; it emphasizes the gravity of the problem with which we are faced. The further argument is made that the boys who enlisted under age are personally to blame because they described themselves as being older than they were. Surely the medical examiners would not pass 5,000 boys who were under age -that is	a very large number.
If true, it certainly does not reflect much credit on the medical examiners. I can easily understand that a great many would get through. I know boys personally who enlisted when under age and who were quite well known to be under age by the military authorities who accepted them. The cost of training 5,000 boys at $1,000 each would be $5,000,000, and- what the House and the Government must consider is this: Is it worth $5,000,000 to take 5,000 boys out of the cesspool of ignorance and put them on the highway to decency and capability? In justification I may say it is not my fault I did not get the right figures. I think if the minister had given me about two hours in his office I could have got the figures exactly. I am sure they must be easily available on short notice, and I cannot understand why the figures have not been given in answer to the question I asked over two weeks ago. At all events, the Bill is in preparation and

I am willing at the request of the Government to withdraw this resolution at present. But in all courtesy and in a perfectly kind spirit, I am going to advise the Government that if the principle of this resolution is not included in the Bill when brought down I shall exercise my freedom as a citizen of Canada and as a member of this House to fight the Bill to a finish, because I feel this is too important a matter to be lightly dealt with. I do not say that with any desire to harass the Government, but I think the expression of opinion here tonight should be quite sufficient for the Government to include such a provision in the Bill as is sought by this resolution. I wish to thank the Government for saying they are going to bring down the Bill.

speechtext:
For a copy of all papers, records, and other documents, In the case of His Majesty the King, Appellant, and Pierre Edouard Emile Belanger! Respondent, now pending in the Supreme Court of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, last year on two occasions I brought this matter before the House, and I wish now just to point out very briefly the facts of this case. As you are aware* some years ago the Government decided to build a dam on the River St. Charles at Quebec. A gentleman by the name of Belanger was the proprietor of two beach lots on the River St. Charles, and when the time came to build the dam in question expropriation proceedings were taken, and a petition was entered before the Exchequer Court, where the respondent Belanger, who was the plaintiff in the court below, claimed from the Government the sum of $800,000 in round figures; this seemingly representing 50 cents per square foot for one of the two lots and 35 cents per square foot for the other. His Majesty the King was represented in this case by a very eminent counsel from Levis, Mr. Bernier, who has been the batonnier of the bar in that district and, if I mistake not, for the whole province of Quebec. Mr. Bernier denied that Belanger had any valid title to these two lots, denied also that the portion of these lots situate between high and low water marks were always water lots situate in the estuary of the River St. Charles and covered with the waters thereof, and affirmed that said lots always formed part of the Crown lands and were never legally granted to anybody. That was one of the
pleas filed by the Crown as represented by its counsel. Then it was averred that even if the respondent proved his title, a reasonable sum ascertained under the provisions of the Expropriation Act should be paid him for the value of such lands and the damages resulting therefrom. The enquete took place. Mr. Justice Audette of the Exchequer Court, went to Quebec and quite an array of witnesses was summoned before him. Finally, on the 28th of June, 1917, judgment was rendered. The Court held that the respondent had proven his title and was entitled to recover the value of the lands. The amount awarded by Mr. Justice Audette for the two lots totalled $215,925.10, with interest. To that amount the judge added the 10 per cent which is allowed in some cases owing to peculiar circumstances. This 10 per cents, at the rate of 10 cents a square foot, represented the sum of $21,592.51. The case was appealed by His Majesty the King and came up before the Supreme Court last year when this Parliament was in session. In his factum the counsel for the Crown stated that the Crown accepted the judgment of the Exchequer Court as regards the larger amount, but appealed as regards the smaller sum of $21,592.51. When the case came up before the Supreme Court one of the judges appeared to be surprised at the way in which it had been conducted, and inquired of counsel if the Crown were really appealing only as regards the smaller award, or as regards the larger sum as well. On counsel insisting *that the appeal was in respect of the smaller sum only, the court of its own initiative stopped the case and decided to ask that new instructions be given to counsel. This attracted my attention .as it appeared in the press, and I was curious enough to look at the record of the case. To my amazement I found some startling developments in it. I discovered that Mr. Justice Audette had reluctantly made the award after witnesses had been heard in the city of Quebec. He said:
The lands in question were acquired by the suppliant for the sum of $18,165.32, and were practically yielding no revenue save the renting of one house on lot 513, and pasture on lot 560. These lots lie in the estuary of the river St. Charles, and are nothing but a stretch of muddy soil upon which in the case of 560 some marine grass grows upon which cattle may feed ; but the land is entirely covered by water at high tide, and the lot has been practically idle and no use has been made of it for years and years. Wharves may he built upon the same, as wharves may be built in fields, but it has no access to deep water, except to the height of the water brought in by the tide. Lot No. 513

is impracticable far building purposes. It is a beach lot. Some of the witnesses were candid enough to say, they thought the property had very little value, but it might have value for public purposes and assessed it on that basis. In other words, that the property was of very little value to the owner, but might toe of Some good value to a party expropriating for public purposes, or for a scheme like the present works. However, it is now settled' law that in assessing compensation for property taken under compulsory powers, it is not proper to consider as port of the market value to the owner such value as the land taken may have to the party expropriating when viewed as an integral part of the proposed work or undertaking.
The Court must guard against fostering speculating in expropriation matters, and must not encourage the making of extravagant claims, and more especially must guard against being carried away by the subtle arguments of real estate speculators or expert witnesses and thus rerider the execution of public works impossible or prohibitive. While the owner must toe amply compensated- in that he shall toe no poorer after the expropriation, it is no reason to charge the public exchequer with exorbitant compensation built upon an imaginary or speculative -basis. These remarks I must confess are provoked by the extravagant amount of the claim of the suppliant, namely the sum of $80-0,0-8-5.65 for a property which cost him, a few years before, the sum of $18,1615.37 as above set forth, and more especially when the property -has been idle for years -and years and the -public work in question herein is the only thing which wil-l give it any value. I feel I am perhaps allowing too high an amount for a -property composed of waste flats and -beach entirely covered with water at high tides, whicih -a -few years ago cost in round figures $18,000 and which -had- fbeen for years practically unproductive and has been a charge upon the owner, the taxes being larger than the revenues, and but for the public work in question would, have very likely remained idle for years to come.
However, the judge rendered his judgment, -and to the sum of [DOT] 8215,925.10 he added 10 per cent for -compulsory taking- because the land had been taken against the owner's will-the total sum being $237,517.61. Now I confess that when I read this judgment, and the appeal therefrom, I w.as startled to find that for a property consisting of two be-ach lots on the -St. Charles river which had cost the owner originally $18,000, and which did not produce enough revenue for years -and years to pay -the taxes, His Majesty the King should pay over $237,000. This was acquired for a public work which, I am informed, has been abandoned.

speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman discovered in the record the evidence upon which the judge based his finding allowing $21-5,000?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext:
I have not the evidence before me, but I had it last year. The evidence, with the plans, is filed in the
[Mr. T.cmieux.l
Supreme Court. The evidence is very lengthy. I found that last year no expert appraiser had been called as a witness. Several neighbours and friends had been called. When the man from whom this property was purchased died his estate had been obliged to pay the inheritance tax to the provincial government and a declaration was filed which, had it been filed in this case, would have proven that the estate attached no value whatsoever to these lots. Yet, that evidence was not adduced before the judge. The judge reluctantly granted that enormous amount of $237,000 for a property which was bought for $18,000 and which for years had not produced enough to pay the taxes.
The judges of the Supreme Court were startled, stopped the case and told the counsel for the Government that he should receive new instructions from the Department of Justice. What I want to know from the Minister of Justice, or his representative, is whether or not new instructions have been issued, whether new evidence has been adduced and just what the Government intends to do in this matter.
With the present financial condition of the country it would be nothing short of scandalous that this enormous amount oi money should be paid to land speculators especially when the object for which the construction was made-a dam-is being abandoned by the -Government. I think the House is entitled to get some explanation from the Government because, as will be shown by the record, this land was bought evidently with the view of carrying on a speculation at the expense of the taxpayers. The Government has been warned. On two occasions last year I called the attention of the House to this case and I am informed that the case was lately given a re-hearing by the Supreme Court. No new instructions were issued. Possibly the judgment may he that the award of the Exchequer Court be confirmed. No doubt it will be confirmed because the Counsel for the Department of Justice accepts the award and contests it only for the smaller amount. It is something remarkable. Here is an award of $237,000 given reluctantly by the judge, as the judge so admitted. Counsel goes before the court, files his factum, introduces his case and says: Oh, well, as regards the large amount of $225,000, the Crown accepts that award, hut as regards the $25,000, we intend to fight. It is a very strange circumstance indeed. The damming of the river St. Charles has been stopped, so I

am informed, and yet this case goes one. Some time next fall somebody will startle the country by stating that the amount has been paid. I do not care one whit wheie it is that the expropriation has taken place. It would be far better for me probably not to say a word. I would be very popular in the neighbourhood if I would remain silent on this question. But I am a taxpayer, I am one of the legislators of Canada, and it is my duty as a legislator and a member of Parliament to protest against such a scandalous transaction. The Government, I repeat, has been warned, but instead of heeding the warning the Government is proceeding with the case and no action has been taken. Well, I give a last warning to the Government and I say: Retrace your steps, and stop this proceeding because it is nothing short of a scandal.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman had spent five minutes telephoning to the Department of Public Works and making inquiry there he would have understood the situation in regard to this matter and he never would have made the speech that he has made this evening. The only reason that I am saying anything in answer to what the hon. gentleman has said is that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) and my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) are absent. I am not seized of all the facts but let me say that I was in Quebec and looked over this property when I was Acting Minister of Public Works. It is true the property was expropriated, but I do not think any Minister of Public Works would have ever considered the purchase of that property even at $18,000. Certainly, I would not myself have taken it at that sum. However, the property was expropriated and the case was sent to the Exchequer Court, which is the customary procedure in expropriation proceedings. The decision of the Exchequer Court is supposed to be satisfactory to all, but what astonishes me, as well as the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, was that the Exchequer Court gave judgment for $215,000. That fact not only surprised me, but it surprised the Government as a whole. I am free to admit that the case was badly handled in the Exchequer Court. I believe that if the Government had been represented by better counsel that judgment would never have been given. An appeal to the Supreme Court followed, and argument was heard in that court. However, the Department of Justice was following the case,
and when it heard in court the position taken by counsel, as stated by the hon. member, a stay of proceedings was applied for and granted. The Department of Justice engaged other counsel and took the case in hand itself. If the hon. gentleman has made inquiries ho must know that the department asked for a new trial, and that a new trial was granted. He must also know if he is acquainted with the facts, that the Department of Public Works has filed a plan abandoning three-quarters of the property for the reason that it does not require it. What will now happen is this: one-fourth of the property has been built on and therefore must be retained, but there will be a valuation of it. Unless we get a fair valuation there will be a further hearing in the Exchequer Court, and the Government will be represented by the best counsel it can get. When the case is tried, and judgment rendered, it will be fair and just. With the full information in his possession, which the hon. gentleman could have got by merely telephoning for it as I did, it would not have been necessary to have taken up the time of the House for one hour to-night trying to make it appear that there has been an awful scandal, whereas the facts are that three-quarters of the property that was sought to be foisted on the Government have been abandoned, that only twenty-five per cent of the property is being retained, for which a fair value will be paid, and that instead of $215,000 having been paid out not one dollar has been expended.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext:
I know something of the circumstances of this case, and I know the counsel who was employed by the Government. That counsel has been the Batonnier of the Bar of Quebec, Baton-nier General of the province of Quebec, mayor of the city of Levis, member in the Quebec Legislature for the County of Levis, and is one of the most respected lawyers at the Bar of Quebec. Last year when this question came up, the Minister of Justice made this reply to an interpelation by the member for Maisonneuve (Air. Lemieux):
t There Is not any doubt that the Crown was represented by counsel. The facts in regard to the direct action of the Crown are that the instructions were of the clearest possible kind, that an appeal should be made from the entire award, and the appeal which was lodged under the immediate direction of the Deputy Minister of Justice, as the departmental records will certainly show, was an appeal from the entire award.
The documents which will be filed will show that the appeal was not for the entire

award, but for the ten per cent specially provided in the award by the judge of the Exchequer Court.
Mr. J. D. RlEID: It may be true that the appeal to the 'Supreme Court was made in the way that the hon. gentleman states, but it was the lawyer from Levis who made it, not the Justice Department.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext: Under whose instructions?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext:
I will come to that point,
because I have something more in store for the hon. minister. The Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) now acknowledges that the appeal was only for the ten per -cent, and yet the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), when giving information to this House last year, said that the appeal had been made under the direction of the Deputy Minister of Justice and for the full award. We now have the evidence that the appeal was not made for the full award, but only for the ten per cent. There is something further. The hon. gentleman says the appeal was made only for the ten per cent, but it was made thorugh counsel who did not obey his instructions. Well, Sir, a few days after the session
11	pjm. closed-and the statement to which I have referred was given to the House by the Minister of Justice on the 23rd of May, 1918, the very day of prorogation-I returned to Quebec and had an interview with Mr. Bernier himself. He then told me definitely that he had written instructions to appeal only for the ten per cent. There is something very mysterious about this case. I have not the slightest doubt that the counsel engaged by the Crown to act in these proceedings tells the truth when he says he had written instructions, and it simply envelops the whole affair in greater mystery. This is particularly true when we remember that the Minister of Justice made the statement last year that the appeal was for the full award, whereas to-day we have the evidence that it was not for the full award but only for the ten per cent.
I say, Sir, that this case is really tantamount to a big scandal. It is a scandal to see the Minister of Justice give wrong information to the House on a matter of such importance. Before giving the information he should have taken steps to verify it. I am not going so far as to say that he deliberately gave wrong information, but surely when a minister of the Crown is giving an answer to a question put to him
rAir. Vien.]
in this House his answer should be based on first-hand knowledge. It is also .mysterious and almost tantamount to a scandal for a minister of the Crown to say that he gave instructions and that the appeal was for the full award, when the counsel who was retained by the Government to deal with this matter

and who is a reliable member of the Quebec Bar, one who has occupied the highest position in its gift- definitely states that he acted on the written instructions of the department. I submit that it is time we saw the bottom, and the under bottom, of the whole affair, and it seems to me that the Government should lay on the Table all the documents bearing on this case, so that we can investigate the matter fully and call to account during this session the people responsible, and not wait, as they did last year, until the last day of the session before producing the evidence.
Mr. D. D. McrvENZIE: I do not mink that the Government should get off lightly on this transaction. I have facing me on the front benches of the Government four distinguished members of the Bar, and this is a legal question. I am surprised that when proceedings in the Exchequer Court and in the Supreme Court of Canada are under fire my good friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) is put forth as the chief bluffer. I do not always agree with the judgment of the leader of the Government, but on this occasion, in putting forth the Minister of Railways in a case of this character his judgment was of the very first order. The Minister of Railways started out bold and aggressive as usual, which is the first essential of a bluffer, but it fell through, Mr. Speaker, it was not half as effective as I thought it was going to be. we are now down to the rock bottom of this business, and the Government must give an account to this House and to the country as to how it is that some $250,000 of public money was almost paid, tne judgment of one court delivered and almost the judgment of another, until the court itself stopped making it obligatory on the people to pay out this sum of money.
What should the Government have done about this case? I was never a minister, and possibly I never shall be, but I know what the procedure is in matters of this kind. When the Government wants land it is supposed to send a competent Government surveyor to inspect the site, make a plan of the land required and report on its value. In this case we find that after the matter has gone through the courts and we have almost paid $250,000, it is dis-

covered that it is only a quarter of the land that they want. Is that good business, is that the kind of procedure that this Government will countenance? They never even procured an estimate of the value oi the land. Having obtained a report and valuation the department should have tendered the money to the owner of the land. Was that done in this case? The Minister of Railways said to-night that he went on the ground as a casual observer, that he was merely acting on behalf of some other minister, that he considered it was ridiculous to pay the sum of money that had been suggested. The department should have obtained a valuation of the land, tendered the owner the amount of the valuation, and if he refused to take the amount he could go to the Exchequer Court at his own risk, for if the Exchequer Court found the property was not worth any more than the amount tendered, he would have to pay the cost of the proceedings. That is the way this business should have been carried through.
L submit, that there was the greatest possible bungling and negligence in this transaction, from start to finish that ever came before this House, and that this attempt to bluff it off is something not worthy of consideration. I think it is hardly fair to the lawyer who acted in the case, who was not instructed fully as to the facts, and who was evidently made a scapegoat to allow this business to go through to answer some sinister motive that evidently some speculator in touch with partisan authority had in mind in the whole transaction. There is not a word of evidence here from the Government that the lawyer concerned ever had the proper data put in his hands, and I submit that it is hardly fair to him to hold him responsible for the whole business, when the Government itself and those responsible were derelict.
It seems to me, Sir, that we are very much indebted to the honourable member who has brought this matter to the notice of the House, and I do hope that even at this late day the Government knows how much of this land it wants, and that it will have a proper appraisement made of its worth, and will tender the money to the owner and let him take the responsibility of disputing the value in the Exchequer Court. The whole transaction is something that the responsible department should apologize for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that
the Acting Minister of Justice is not in his
seat to-night. He was not aware that this* Order would be called this evening and he went home some little time ago. I asked the Minister of Railways,-who, as he stated, was at times Acting Minister of Public Works,-to make inquiry of the Deputy Minister of that department with a view to having some information laid before the House to answer the question of my honourable friend.
Personally I know nothing of the transaction. So far as the Government is concerned we are willing that the correspondence called for shall be brought down. Untd the documents are brought down it is rather futile to discuss the matter in the House, because we should have assertion on one hand and counter-assertion on the other, and we should. make no progress toward elucidation of the facts. From the discussion to-night, however, two or three matters seem to me to stand out.
It is stated by the mover of the resolution (Mr. Lemieux), and by the hon. member (Mr. Vien) who has spoken in support of it, that the counsel engaged by the Department of Justice to represent the Crown in the expropriation proceedings before the Exchequer Court is a man of eminent legal ability. That in itself would appear to be conclusive proof that the Government was not, as stated by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) negligent with respect to the proceeding. In a proceeding of importance involving the expropriation of property of considerable value the most important matter is the selection of counsel, and by the admission of those who are making these charges-for they are charges in effect-against the Government here tonight, the counsel selected was a man of high standing at the bar. Before the court of first instance, the trial court, the presentation of matters of fact is of supreme importance because it is upon the evidence adduced there that the court reaches its conclusion, after hearing the witnesses and observing their demeanour, as to the value of the property expropriated. The principal thing in litigation affecting property by expropriation is the decision of the first court, because a court of appeal will not lightly set aside the decision of the court which has heard the evidence, seen the witnesses and reached a conclusion on the facts adduced before it. Nothing is put forward here to suggest that the counsel selected was not a man of standing before the courts of Quebec; on the contrary, he has been vouched for by the two hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken.



The Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) has said that he saw the property in question before or about the time that the expropriation proceedings were had. He was of the view that it was not worth more than $18,000. He could not well know what the court would determine it was worth; therefore his view of the transaction at that time would be in accordance with his judgment as to what the value of the property was. The St. Charles works were projected in 1012 upon a larger scale than that upon which they have been or will be carried on. One can conceive ol a piece of property, not regarded as of great value, being expropriated in connection with a larger project and the conclusion being reached, upon that project being reduced, that a part of the property might be abandoned, as the Minister of Railways said to-night. It has been suggested by the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) that the Minister of Justice misled the House. I am sure he would not say that the Minister of Justice intentionally misled the House. Tire Minister of Justice made a statement which I am certain he made in all good faith, and if it is In fact an error-I do not pronounce upon that, as I do not know the facts-I am ;ure that it was made by inadvertence. He was speaking of an appeal from the Exchequer Court judgment to the Supreme Court. Now it has been stated that a new Irial has been granted at the instance of the Department of Justice. That new trial was sought, no doubt, on the ground of the judgment that was rendered by the Exchequer Court and which was on appeal before the Supreme Court. If a new trial has been granted, as stated, and if three ' quarters of the property has been abandoned, it seems to me, looking at the entire transaction in the light of what I have said, that there is nothing to call for any particular censure of the Government. Eminent counsel selected; judgment given; appeal had to the Supreme Court; new trial asked and granted; the project as originally conceived reduced; three-quarters of the property taken abandoned, one-quarter only retained; issue now as to the value of that one-quarter. That seems to be the position of the transaction at present. As I stated at the outset, the Government will be very glad to bring down the papers, and until they are brought down I do not think the House can reach any ust conclusion with regard to the transaction or as to allegations made by hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext:
If the facts were as argued by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White), the. case would not be very good, though it would still have a leg to stand upon. But I am afraid that the case is not exactly as he would like it to be. As it stands, the case is as follows: The Government of Canada decides to build a dam on the river St. Charles, and has to expropriate some land in order to do so. I am credibly informed that the two lots in question are below the dam, not above the dam; therefore they are not at all affected by the dam. That is the first information I get. Moreover, many speculators are involved in this case; there is an Ethiopian in the pile. I am informed that this man Belanger is only a prete-nom -a name borrowed lr others. First of all, there is a petition of right, and action is taken before the Exchequer Court, and expropriation proceedings are had. Does it not strike you that there is something radically wrong with this business? For a property for which the owner is supposed to have paid $18,000, the judge, according to his own words, reluctantly grants $237,000. No expert appraisers are called; the judge is helpless; he looks around; who is going to enlighten him? The Department of Justice should have keen to that. Think of the enormity of the case! Here is a man claiming $800,000 for a property that cost him $18,000, and which had not produced enough revenue to pay the taxes during a period of twenty years. There is something" strikingly strange about that. The judge after having heard the witnesses, with the acquiescence of the counsel representing the Government, renders judgment. An appeal is taken by the Department of Justice. The interests of the Crown are again confided to this same counsel. Now I hope that when the papers are filed, the letter of protest written by Mr. Bernier, K.C., will be filed with them because he declares most emphatically that he received his instructions from the Department of Justice to appeal only from the smaller amount, the 10 per cent, and not from the larger amount, $225,000. At all events no case is filed in the Supreme Court in tvhich His Majesty the King is involved without the Minister or Deputy Minister of Justice surveying the whole case. How does it happen that this factum was filed with this declaration on behalf of the Grown?
By the judgment of the Exchequer Court rendered on the 28th day of June, 1917, the Court held that the respondent had proven his title and was entitled to reoover the value of the land expropriated from him by the appellant.

Prom this part of -the Judgment of the Exchequer Court the appellant does'not appeal.
The appellant is His Majesty the King, represented by the Minister of Justice or by the Deputy Minister of Justice. I had the honour of being Solicitor General of Canada for two years and I know, and everybody knows, that no document issues from the Department of Justice for any of the courts, whether it be the Exchequer Court, the Supreme Court, or any other, without first being surveyed and passed on by the Minister of Justice or at least by the very able Deputy Minister of Justice, Mr. Newcombe.
My hon. friend says that the honour of the counsel is not questioned. It is not. It has never been questioned by me or by anybody else; but I say to the Government that there is something very mysterious in the whole proceeding; there is something very mysterious which must be clarified by the Government. The Minister of Railways and Canals says that a new trial has been ordered. How does he know?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext:
I inquired over the
telephone from the Deputy Minister of Public Works-the Minister of Public Works was away-and the information I have given to the House is what I got from him over the telephone just a few moments ago.
Mr. jLEMIEUX : I am sorry, but I think my hon. friend has been misinformed, not intentionally so, by the Deputy Minister of Public Works. My hon. friend should have inquired from the Deputy Minister of Justice, because the case is conducted by the Department of Justice, and not by the Department of Public Works. I am informed by some one who was present at the Supreme Court a few weeks ago when this same case was argued-argued, if 1 mistake not, by Mr. Chrysler, K.C., the very eminent counsel from Ottawa-that Mr. Chrysler took no different stand from that taken by Mr. Bernier; he argued from the same evidence, from the same factum, and
there was no change in the procedure. The case is now en delibere by the Supreme Court and I am very much surprised at the information the minister has just given.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext:
The Deputy Minister
of Public Works tells me the Supreme Court has granted a new trial.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ST. CHARLES RIVER IMPROVEMENTS -THE KING V. BELANGER.
speechtext: I have followed the proceedings of the Supreme Court for the last few days and have read some of the judgments, but I am not aware that the Supreme Court has granted judgment in this case. But if it has, well and good. If a new trial has been granted, well and good. A new trial will be highly gratifying to me, and I am pleased to learn that the Government has at last awakened to the enormity of this claim. I am glad the Government has reduced by 75 per cent the acreage required for the damming of the river St. Charles, and I can assure my hon. friend that when this case comes up, if a new trial has been granted, the Government's counsel may obtain from the provincial revenue officers in Quebec the clearest possible evidence that this property is worth just a few hundred dollars. My hon. friend seemed a little excited when he spoke a few moments ago, but he should not have been excited. He should have thanked me for bringing this matter before the House. I brought it up last year on two occasions without any result. I could get no information then; but to-night I learn that a new trial has been asked for by the Department of Public Works and has been granted by the Court, and that the department will not require more than 25 per cent of the two lots. Well, I think that is a success, and under the circumstances my motion should pass unanimously and with cheers.

Motion agreed to.
-On motion of Sir Thomas White the House adjourned at 11.40 p.m..
